<!-- theorema-1: body_md -->
\label{ThmA}
Let $\beta\,:\, H\curvearrowright B$ be an ergodic action, $G$ any compact quantum group with dual quantum subgroup $F$ and define $\mathbb{G}:=G\wr_{*,\beta,F}H$. The following holds.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\widehat{\mathbb{G}}$ is exact if and only if both $\widehat{G}$ and $\widehat{H}$ are exact.
    \item If ${\rm Irr}(F)$ is finite, $\widehat{\mathbb{G}}$ has the Haagerup property if and only if both $\widehat{G}$ and $\widehat{H}$ have the Haagerup property.
    \item $\mathbb{G}$ is Kac if and only if both $G$ and $H$ are Kac and in this case, assuming that $F$ is coamenable, $\widehat{\mathbb{G}}$ is hyperlinear if and only if both $\widehat{G}$ and $\widehat{H}$ are hyperlinear.
    \item If $F$ is trivial and both $G$ and $H$ are non-trivial then $\mathbb{G}$ is coamenable if and only if $G=H=\mathbb{Z}_2$ and $B\in\{\mathbb{C},\mathbb{C}^2\}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorema-1 -->
<!-- theorema-2: body_md -->
\label{ThmB}
Suppose that $\beta$ is $2$-ergodic, both $G$ and $H$ are infinite quantum groups and $F$ is trivial then ${\rm L}^\infty(\mathbb{G})$ is a non amenable factor of type ${\rm II}_1$ or ${\rm III}$ and its $T$ invariant is:
$$T({\rm L}^\infty(\mathbb{G}))=\{t\in\mathbb{R}\,:\,\sigma_t^{h_G}={\rm id}\text{ and }\sigma_t^{h_H}={\rm id}\}.$$
where $\sigma_t^{h_G}$ is the modular group of the Haar state of $G$ (and the same for $H$). Moreover ${\rm L}^\infty(\mathbb{G})$ is of type ${\rm II}_1$ if and only if both $G$ and $H$ are Kac.
<!-- end theorema-2 -->
<!-- theorema-3: body_md -->
\label{ThmC}
Suppose that ${\rm dim}(B)\geq 3$, $\beta$ is $2$-ergodic, both $G$ and $H$ are infinite quantum groups and $F$ is trivial then the following holds.
\begin{enumerate}
\item ${\rm L}^\infty(\mathbb{G})$ is prime.
\item ${\rm L}^\infty(\mathbb{G})$ has no Cartan subalgebras.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorema-3 -->
<!-- theorema-4: body_md -->
\label{thmD}
Let $\beta\,:\,H\curvearrowright B$ be any ergodic action, $G$ any compact quantum group with dual quantum subgroup and $\mathbb{G}:=G\wr_{*,\beta,F}H$ the free wreath product. The following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\widehat{G}$ and $\widehat{H}$ are $K$-amenable.
\item $\widehat{\mathbb{G}}$ is $K$-amenable.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorema-4 -->
<!-- theorema-5: body_md -->
\label{ThmE}
For all $s,N\in\mathbb{N}^*$ and for any faithful state $\psi\in M_N(\mathbb{C})^*$ one has:
$$K_i(C_\bullet(\mathbb{Z}_s\wr_*{\rm Aut}^+(M_N(\mathbb{C}),\psi)))=\left\{\begin{array}{lcl}\mathbb{Z}^s\oplus\mathbb{Z}_N&\text{if}&i=0,\\\mathbb{Z}&\text{if}&i=1.\end{array}\right.\quad\text{and,}$$
$$K_i(C_\bullet(\widehat{\mathbb{F}}_s\wr_*{\rm Aut}^+(M_N(\mathbb{C}),\psi)))=\left\{\begin{array}{lcl}\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_N&\text{if}&i=0,\\\mathbb{Z}^{s+1}&\text{if}&i=1.\end{array}\right.$$
<!-- end theorema-5 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{RmkReducedUcp}
Let $\varphi\,:\, A\rightarrow B$ be a ucp map with reduced C*-algebra and GNS-morphism $\pi\,:\,A\twoheadrightarrow C^*_r(\varphi)$ and let $\varphi_r\,:\,C^*_r(\varphi)\rightarrow B$ be the unique GNS-faithful ucp map such that $\varphi_r\circ\pi=\varphi$. If $\varphi_r$ is faithful then, for any unital C*-subalgebra $A_0\subset A$ one has $C^*_r(\varphi\vert_{A_0})=\pi(A_0)$. It is a direct consequence of the uniqueness of the reduced C*-algebra of a ucp map since $\varphi_r\vert_{A_0}$ is still faithful hence GNS-faithful.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{LemOneParameter}
Fix a faithful normal state (f.n.s.) $\mu\in N_*$ and assume that $\mu\circ\gamma_t=\mu$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$. Then $\tau$ is a strongly continuous one parameter group of $M$ preserving $\mu\circ E_N$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Define the f.n.s. $\omega=\mu\circ E_N\in M_*$ and note that, for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and $x\in M$, $\omega\circ\tau_t(x)=\omega(x)$. Indeed, the equality is clear when $x$ is reduced and for $x\in N$ it follows from the hypothesis $\mu\circ\gamma_t=\mu$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$. Define $X:=\{x\in M\,:\,(t\mapsto\tau_t(x))\text{ is strongly continuous}\}$ and note that $X$ is a vector subspace, stable by involution and contains $M_1\cup M_2$. Let $x,y\in X$ and let us show that $xy\in X$. View $M\subset\mathcal{L}({\rm L}^2(M,\omega))$, where $\xi_\omega$ is the cyclic vector in the GNS construction ${\rm L}^2(M,\omega)$ of $\omega$. One has, for all $s,t\in\mathbb{R}$, $\tau_t(xy)-\tau_s(xy)=\tau_t(x)(\tau_t(y)-\tau_s(y))+(\tau_t(x)-\tau_s(y))\tau_s(y)$. Hence, for all $\xi\in H$, and all sequence $(t_n)_n$ converging to $t$ one has:
$$\Vert(\tau_{t_n}(xy)-\tau_{t}(xy))\xi\Vert\leq\Vert x\Vert\,\Vert(\tau_{t_n}(y)-\tau_t(y))\xi\Vert+\Vert(\tau_{t_n}(x)-\tau_t(x))\tau_t(y)\xi\Vert\rightarrow_n0$$
since both $x,y\in X$. It follows that $X$ is a subalgebra of $M$ containing both $M_1$ and $M_2$. Hence, it suffices to show that $X$ is strong* closed in $M$. Let $(x_n)_n\in X$ be a sequence converging strongly to $x\in M$ (in particular, $(x_n)$ is norm bounded). It suffices to show that the set $$Z:=\{\xi\in {\rm L}^2(M,\omega)\,:\,(t\mapsto\tau_t(x)\xi)\text{ is continuous }\}$$
is equal to ${\rm L}^2(M,\omega)$. Let $\xi=a\xi_\omega$, where $a\in M$ is analytic with respect to the modular group $(\sigma_t)_t$ of $\omega$. Denoting by $J$ the anti-unitary modular operator of $\omega$ we have,
\begin{eqnarray*}
\Vert\tau_t(x_n)\xi-\tau_t(x)\xi\Vert&=&\Vert\tau_t(x_n-x)a\xi_\omega\Vert=\Vert\tau_t(x_n-x)J\sigma_{i/2}(a)^*J\xi_\omega\Vert\\
&=&\Vert J\sigma_{i/2}(a)^*J\tau_t(x_n-x)\xi_\omega\Vert\leq\Vert\sigma_{i/2}(a)\Vert\Vert\tau_t(x_n-x)\xi_\omega\Vert\\
&=&\Vert\sigma_{i/2}(a)\Vert\cdot\omega(\tau_t((x_n-x)^*(x_n-x)))^{1/2}\\
&=&\Vert\sigma_{i/2}(a)\Vert\cdot\omega((x_n-x)^*(x_n-x))^{1/2}.
\end{eqnarray*}
It follows that the sequence of continuous maps $(t\mapsto\sigma_t(x_n)\xi)_n$ converges uniformly on $\mathbb{R}$ to the map $t\mapsto\sigma_t(x)\xi$. Hence, $a\xi_\omega\in Z$ for all $a\in M$ analytic with respect to $(\sigma_t)_t$. Since this set is dense in ${\rm L}^2(M,\omega)$, it suffices to show that $Z$ is norm-closed in ${\rm L}^2(M,\omega)$. Let $\xi_n\in Z$ be a sequence converging to $\xi\in{\rm L}^2(M,\omega)$. Writing $\Vert\tau_t(x)\xi_n-\tau_t(x)\xi\Vert\leq\Vert x\Vert\Vert\xi_n-\xi\Vert$, we can argue as before to deduce that $\xi\in Z$. It concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{RmkModularFree}
Let $\mu\in N_*$ be any f.n.s. and define $\varphi_k:=\mu\circ E_k\in (M_k)_*$ and $\varphi:=\mu\circ E_N\in M_*$. The following relation between the modular groups of $\varphi$, $\varphi_1$ and $\varphi_2$ is shown in \cite{Ue99}: $\sigma^\varphi=\sigma^{\varphi_1}*\sigma^{\varphi_2}$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
If $\omega$ is almost periodic on a diffuse von Neumann algebra $M$ then its centralizer is diffuse. Indeed, if $p\in M^\omega$ is a (non-zero) minimal projection, then the centralizer of the f.n.s. on $pMp$ given $\varphi:=\omega(p)^{-1}\omega(p\cdot p)$ is $M^\varphi=pM^\omega p=\mathbb{C} p$. It follows that, for all $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$ and all $x\in V^\varphi_\lambda$, $x^*x\in V^\varphi_\lambda V^\varphi_{\lambda^{-1}}\subset M^\varphi=\mathbb{C} p$. Hence, $V_\varphi\subset \mathbb{C} p$ and, since $\omega$ is almost periodic, $\varphi$ is almost periodic on $pMp$ so $pMp=\mathbb{C} p$ and $p$ is minimal in $M$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{dualqsg}
Let $G$ and $F$ be CQG. The following data are equivalent.
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\iota\,:\, C(F)\rightarrow C(G)$ is a faithful unital $*$-homomorphism intertwining the comultiplications.
    \item $\iota\,:\,{\rm Pol}(F)\rightarrow{\rm Pol}(G)$ is a faithful unital $*$-homomorphism intertwining the comultiplications.
    \item $\iota\,:\,C_r(F)\rightarrow C_r(G)$ is a faithful unital $*$-homomorphism intertwining the comultiplications.
\end{itemize} If one of the following equivalent conditions is satisfied, we view ${\rm Pol}(F)\subset{\rm Pol}(G)$, $C(F)\subset C(G)$ and $C_r(F)\subset C_r(G)$. Then, the unique linear map $E_F\,:\,{\rm Pol}(G)\rightarrow {\rm Pol}(F)$ such that
$$({\rm id}\otimes E_F)(u^x)=\left\{\begin{array}{lcl}u^x&\text{if}&x\in{\rm Irr}(F),\\0&\text{if}&x\in{\rm Irr}(G)\setminus{\rm Irr}(F).\end{array}\right.$$
has a unique ucp extension to a map $E_F\,:\,C(G)\rightarrow C(F)$ which is a Haar-state-preserving conditional expectation onto the subalgebra $C(F)\subset C(G)$. Hence, there exists a unique conditional expectation $E_F^r\,:\, C_r(G)\rightarrow C_r(F)$ such that $E_F^r\circ\lambda_G=\lambda_F\circ E_F$. Moreover, $E^r_F$ is faithful and Haar-state-preserving and extends to a Haar-state preserving normal faithful conditional expectation $E_F''\,:\,{\rm L}^\infty(G)\rightarrow{\rm L}^\infty(F)$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{RmkEF} The following holds.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Note that, since $\lambda_G$ is surjective, $E_F^r$ is faithful and $E^r_F\circ\lambda_G=\lambda_F\circ E_F$, $C_r(\mathbb{G})$ is actually the reduced C*-algebra of the ucp map $\lambda_F\circ E_F$ i.e. $C_r(\mathbb{G})=C^*_r(\lambda_F\circ E_F)$.
\item If $a\in{\rm Pol}(G)$ and $E_F(a)=0$ then we can write $\Delta(a)$ as a finite sum $\Delta(a)=\sum_k a_k\otimes b_k$ with $a_k,b_k\in{\rm Pol}(G)$ and $E_F(a_k)=0=E_F(b_k)$ for all $k$. Indeed, assuming that $a\neq 0$ and since $a\in{\rm Pol}(G)$, there exists a finite subset $S\subset{\rm Irr}(G)$ and non-zero $\lambda^x_{ij}\in\mathbb{C}$, $1\leq i,j\leq{\rm dim}(x)$ such that $a=\sum_{x\in S,i,j}\lambda^x_{ij}u^x_{ij}$. Then, $\Delta(a)=\sum_{x\in S,i,j}\lambda^x_{i,j,s} u^x_{is}\otimes u^x_{sj}$ and $E_F(a)=\sum_{x\in S\cap{\rm Irr}(F),i,j}\lambda^x_{ij}u^x_{ij}$. Since $E_F(a)=0$ and coefficients of representations $u^x$ for $x\in{\rm Irr}(G)$ form a basis of ${\rm Pol}(G)$, we deduce that $S\subset{\rm Irr}(G)\setminus{\rm Irr}(F)$.
\item $E_F$ is the unique Haar state preserving conditional expectation, at the full, reduced, von Neumann or algebraic level. Indeed, if $E\,:\, C(G)\rightarrow C(F)$ is a conditional expectation preserving the Haar states then there exists a unique conditional expectation $E^r\,:\, C_r(G)\rightarrow C_r(F)$ such that $E^r\circ\lambda_G=\lambda_F\circ E$ and $E^r$ still preserves the Haar states. By faithfulness of the Haar states at the reduced level, we deduce that $E^r=E^r_F$. Indeed, $h_F((E^r_F(x)-E^r(x))b)=h_F(E_F^r(xb))-h_F(E^r(xb))=h_G(xb)-h_G(xb)=0$ for all $b\in C_r(F)$ and all $x\in C_r(G)$. Since $h_F$ is faithful on $C_r(F)$ it gives the result. It implies that $E=E_F$ on ${\rm Pol}(G)$ and so $E=E_F$ on $C(G)$. For the reduced, von Neumann and algebraic level, the statement is clear since the Haar states are faithful in those cases.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{LemRepAction}
Given any action $\psi$-preserving action $\beta\,:\, B\rightarrow B\otimes C(H)$ the associated unitary representation $u\in\mathcal{L}(B)\otimes C(H)$ satisfies:
\begin{itemize}
\item $u$ is unitary representation of $H$ on $B$.
\item $m\in\mathrm{Mor}_H(u\otimes u,u)$.
\item $\eta\in\mathrm{Mor}_H(1,u)$.
\item $u(L_B(b)\otimes 1)u^*=(L_B\otimes{\rm id})(\beta(b))$ for all $b\in B$.
\item The action $\beta$ is faithful if and only if $C(H)$ is generated by the coefficients of $u$.
\item The action $\beta$ is ergodic if and only if $\mathrm{Mor}_H(1,u)=\mathbb{C}\eta$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{RmkConjugate}
Let $u\in\mathcal{L}(B)\otimes C(H)$ be the representation associated to a $\psi$-preserving action $\beta\,:\, H\curvearrowright B$ then $u\simeq\overline{u}$. Indeed, it is easy to check that $s_u=s_{\overline{u}}:=m^\star\eta\in{\rm Mor}(1,u\otimes u)$ is a pair solving the conjugate equation of $(u,u)$, where $m^\star\,:\, B\rightarrow B\otimes B$ is the adjoint of $m$ with respect to the $\psi$-scalar product on $B$.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{RmkSpectralDecomposition}
 The positive operator $mm^\star$ is actually diagonal in the orthonormal basis $(b^\kappa_{rs})$ of $B$. Indeed, a direct computation shows that $mm^\star(b^\kappa_{rs})={\rm Tr}(Q_\kappa^{-1})b^\kappa_{rs}$ for all $\kappa,r,s$. Writing $\delta_1,\dots\delta_n>0$ the pairwise distinct values taken by ${\rm Tr}(Q_\kappa^{-1})$ we see that ${\rm Sp}(mm^\star)=\{\delta_1,\dots,\delta_n\}$ and, as C*-algebras, $B=\bigoplus_i B_i$, where
$$B_i:={\rm Span}\{b^\kappa_{rs}\,:\,1\leq\kappa\leq K\text{ such that }{\rm Tr}(Q_\kappa^{-1})=\delta_i,\,1\leq r,s\leq N_\kappa\}=\bigoplus_{\kappa,{\rm Tr} (Q_\kappa^{-1})=\delta_i}M_{N_\kappa}(\mathbb{C})$$
is the $\delta_i$-eigenspace of $mm^\star$.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{remadelta}\label{ergodelta}
The following holds.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textit{$\psi$ is a $\delta$-form $\Leftrightarrow$  $\kappa\mapsto{\rm Tr}(Q_\kappa^{-1})$ is constant and in that case $\delta={\rm Tr}(Q_\kappa^{-1})$ $\forall\kappa$. In general, writing $B=\bigoplus B_i$, each $\psi_i:=\frac{1}{\psi(1_{B_i})}\psi\vert_{B_i}$ is a $\delta_i$-form on $B_i$.}

\noindent It is a direct consequence of Remark \ref{RmkSpectralDecomposition}.

\item \textit{$\beta_B\,:\,{\rm Aut}^+(B,\psi)\curvearrowright B$ is always faithful and $\beta_B$ is ergodic if and only if  $\psi$ is a $\delta$-form.}

\noindent Indeed, if $\psi$ is a $\delta$-form then it is known \cite{Ba99,Ba02,Br13} that ${\mathrm{Mor}}(1,u)=\mathbb{C}\eta$ so $\beta_B$ is ergodic. If $\psi$ is not a $\delta$-form then, by the spectral decomposition from Remark \ref{RmkSpectralDecomposition}, $n\geq 2$ and, for $1\leq i\neq j\leq n$, one has $\delta_i\neq \delta_j$ so that $p_i\eta$ and $p_j\eta\in B$ are linearly independent since $1_B=\sum_{\kappa,r}\lambda_\kappa^{-1/2}b^\kappa_{rr}$ which gives $p_k(1_B)=\sum_{\kappa,\,{\rm Tr}(Q_\kappa^{-1})=\delta_k}\lambda_\kappa^{-1/2}b^\kappa_{rr}$ for all $1\leq k\leq n$. Note that, since $mm^\star$ is in the C*-algebra ${\rm End}(u)\subset\mathcal{L}(B)$, we also have $p_k\in{\rm End}(u)$ for all $k$. Hence, $p_i\eta,p_j\eta\in{\rm Mor}(1,u)$ which implies that $\beta_B$ is not ergodic.

\item \textit{For any $\psi$-preserving action $\beta\,:\,H\curvearrowright B$, if $\beta$ is ergodic then $\psi$ is a $\delta$-form.}

\noindent Indeed, assume that $\psi$ is not a $\delta$-form and write $\pi\,:\,C({\rm Aut}^+(B,\psi))\rightarrow C(H)$ the canonical map intertwining the comultiplications and such that $({\rm id}\otimes\pi)\beta_B=\beta$. In particular, $B^{{\rm Aut}^+(B,\psi)}\subseteq B^H$. By $(2)$, $\beta_B$ is not ergodic so ${\rm dim}(B^{{\rm Aut}^+(B,\psi)})\geq 2$ which implies that $\beta$ is not ergodic either.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{PropQAut}
Let $\beta\,:\, H\curvearrowright B$ be an ergodic action on the finite dimensional C*-algebra $B$ with unique invariant state $\psi\in B^*$ and associated representation $u\in\mathcal{L}(B)\otimes C(H)$. The following holds.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $h(u^{ij,\kappa}_{kl,\gamma})=\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}(\lambda_{\kappa,i}\lambda_{\gamma,k})^{\frac{1}{2}}$.
\item $Q_u$ is the positive modular operator $\nabla_\psi$ of $\psi$. In particular,
\begin{enumerate}
\item ${\rm dim}_q(u)=\delta$.
\item $\sigma^h_t(u^{ij,\kappa}_{kl,\gamma})=\left(\frac{\lambda_{\gamma,k}\lambda_{\kappa,i}}{\lambda_{\gamma,l}\lambda_{\kappa,j}}\right)^{it}u^{ij,\kappa}_{kl,\gamma}$ and
$({\rm id}\otimes\sigma^h_t)\circ\beta=(\sigma_t^\psi\otimes{\rm id})\circ\beta\circ\sigma_t^\psi$.
\item $\tau^h_t(u^{ij,\kappa}_{kl,\gamma}) = \left(\frac{\lambda_{\gamma,l}\lambda_{\kappa,i}}{\lambda_{\gamma,k}\lambda_{\kappa,j}}\right)^{it}u^{ij,\kappa}_{kl,\gamma}$ and
$({\rm id}\otimes\tau^h_t)\circ\beta=(\sigma_t^\psi\otimes{\rm id})\circ\beta\circ\sigma_{-t}^{\psi}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
\noindent$(1)$. Since $({\rm id}\otimes h)(u)$ is the orthogonal projection onto ${\rm Mor}(1,u)=\mathbb{C}\eta$ and $\Vert\eta\Vert^2=\psi(1)=1$ one has $({\rm id}\otimes h)(u)=\eta\eta^\star$. Writing $\eta=\sum_{\kappa,i}\lambda_{\kappa,i}^{\frac{1}{2}}b^\kappa_{ii}$ we have
$$\eta\eta^\star=\sum_{\kappa,\gamma,i,k}b^\kappa_{ii}\circ(b^\gamma_{kk})^\star(\lambda_{\kappa,i}\lambda_{\gamma,k})^{\frac{1}{2}}=({\rm id}\otimes h)(u).$$

\vspace{0.2cm}

\noindent$(2)$. Recall from Remark \ref{RmkConjugate} that the pair $(m^\star\eta,m^\star\eta)$ solves the conjugate equation for $(u,u)$. Let us show, under the hypothesis of ergodicity, that the pair $(m^\star\eta,m^\star\eta)$ is standard. It suffices to show that, for all $T\in{\rm End}(u)$, $\varphi_u(T)=\psi_u(T)$, where $\varphi_u(T):=\eta^\star m({\rm id}_B\otimes T)m^\star\eta$ and $\psi_u(T):=\eta^\star m(T\otimes {\rm id}_B)m^\star\eta$. Note that both $m(T\otimes{\rm id}_B)m^\star\eta$ and $m({\rm id}_B\otimes T)m^\star\eta$ are in $\mathrm{Mor}(1,u)$. Since the action is ergodic, there exist $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb{C}$ such that $m(T\otimes{\rm id}_B)m^\star\eta=\lambda\eta$ and $m({\rm id}_B\otimes T)m^\star\eta=\mu\eta$. It suffices to show that $\lambda=\mu$. Write, in the basis of matrix units $(e^\kappa_{ij})_{\kappa,i,j}$ in $\mathcal{L}(B)$ such that $Q_\kappa e^{\kappa}_{ij}=\lambda_{\kappa,i}e^{\kappa}_{ij}$, $T(e^\kappa_{ij})=\sum_{\zeta,k,l}T^{ij,\kappa}_{kl,\zeta}e^\zeta_{kl}$, where $T^{ij,\kappa}_{kl,\zeta}\in\mathbb{C}$ and note that $m^\star\eta=\sum_{\kappa,i,j}\lambda_{\kappa,j}^{-1}e^\kappa_{ij}\otimes e^\kappa_{ji}$. A direct computation gives:
$$m(T\otimes{\rm id}_B)m^\star\eta=\sum_{\kappa,i,j}\left(\sum_k\lambda_{\kappa,k}^{-1}T^{jk,\kappa}_{ik,\kappa}\right)e^\kappa_{ij}\quad\text{and}\quad m({\rm id}_B\otimes T)m^\star\eta=\sum_{\kappa,i,j}\left(\sum_k\lambda_{\kappa,k}^{-1}T^{ki,\kappa}_{kj,\kappa}\right)e^\kappa_{ij}.$$
Since $m(T\otimes{\rm id}_B)m^\star\eta=\lambda \sum_{\kappa,i}e^\kappa_{ii}$ we find that the map $\left[(\kappa,i)\mapsto\sum_k\lambda_{\kappa,k}^{-1}T^{ik,\kappa}_{ik,\kappa}\right]$ is constant, equals to $\lambda$. Similarly, the map $\left[(\kappa,i)\mapsto\sum_k\lambda_{\kappa,k}^{-1}T^{ki,\kappa}_{ki,\kappa}\right]$ is constant, equals to $\mu$. Hence, for all $1\leq\kappa\leq K$ and all $1\leq k\leq N_\kappa$, one has $\mu=\lambda_{\kappa,1}^{-1}T^{1k,\kappa}_{1k,\kappa}+\sum_{i=2}^{N_\kappa}\lambda_{\kappa,i}^{-1}T^{ik,\kappa}_{ik,\kappa}$ which implies that $T^{1k,\kappa}_{1k,\kappa}=\lambda_{\kappa,1}(\mu-\sum_{i=2}^{N_\kappa}\lambda_{\kappa,i}^{-1} T^{ik,\kappa}_{ik,\kappa})$. It follows that:

\begin{eqnarray*}
\lambda&=&\sum_{k=1}^{N_\kappa}\lambda_{\kappa,k}^{-1}T^{1k,\kappa}_{1k,\kappa}=\lambda_{\kappa,1}\sum_{k=1}^{N_\kappa}\lambda_{\kappa,k}^{-1}(\mu-\sum_{i=2}^{N_\kappa}\lambda_{\kappa,i}^{-1} T^{ik,\kappa}_{ik,\kappa})=\lambda_{\kappa,1}\delta\mu-\lambda_{\kappa,1}\sum_{i=2}^{N_\kappa}\lambda_{\kappa,i}^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{N_\kappa}\lambda_{\kappa,k}^{-1}T^{ik,\kappa}_{ik,\kappa}\\
&=&\lambda_{\kappa,1}\delta\mu-\lambda_{\kappa,1}\sum_{i=2}^{N_\kappa}\lambda_{\kappa,i}^{-1}\lambda
=\lambda_{\kappa,1}\delta\mu-\lambda_{\kappa,1}(\delta-\lambda_{\kappa,1}^{-1})\lambda=\lambda_{\kappa,1}\delta(\mu-\lambda)+\lambda.
\end{eqnarray*}

We deduce that $\lambda=\mu$ so $(m^\star\eta,m^\star\eta)$ is standard. It follows that $Q_u=J_u^*J_u$, where $\langle J_u(a),b\rangle=\langle m^\star\eta,a\otimes b\rangle=\langle 1_B,ab\rangle=\psi(ab)=\langle a^*,b\rangle$ for all $a,b\in B$. Hence, $J_u(a)=a^*=S_\psi(a)$, the modular operator of $\psi$. It follows, by definition, that $Q_u=S_\psi^*S_\psi=\nabla_\psi$. Write $S_\psi=J_\psi\nabla^{\frac{1}{2}}_\psi$. A direct computation shows that $J_\psi$ is the unique anti-unitary on $B$ such that $J_\psi(b^\gamma_{kl})=b^\gamma_{lk}$ and $\nabla_\psi(b^\gamma_{kl})=\frac{\lambda_{\gamma,k}}{\lambda_{\gamma,l}}b^\gamma_{kl}$. Hence, ${\rm dim}_q(u)={\rm Tr}(\nabla_\psi)=\sum_\kappa{\rm Tr}(Q_\kappa){\rm Tr}(Q_\kappa^{-1})=\delta\sum_\kappa{\rm Tr}(Q_\kappa)=\delta$. Since $({\rm id}\otimes\sigma_t^h)(u)=(\nabla_\psi^{it}\otimes 1)u(\nabla_\psi^{it}\otimes 1)$, it follows that $({\rm id}\otimes\sigma^h_t)(u)=\sum\left(\frac{\lambda_{\gamma,k}\lambda_{\kappa,i}}{\lambda_{\gamma,l}\lambda_{\kappa,j}}\right)^{it}b^\kappa_{ij}(b^\gamma_{kl})^\star\otimes u^{ij,\kappa}_{kl,\gamma}$ which proves the first part of $(b)$. Moreover, since $\sigma_t^\psi(b)=\nabla_\psi^{it}b\nabla_\psi^{-it}$ for all $b\in B$ we find $\sigma_t^\psi(b^\gamma_{kl})=\left(\frac{\lambda_{\gamma,k}}{\lambda_{\gamma,l}}\right)^{it}b^\gamma_{kl}$ from which we can easily check the last part of $(b)$. $(c)$ is proven the same way using the relation:
\begin{equation*}
    ({\rm id}\otimes \tau_t^h)(u) = (\nabla_\psi^{it}\otimes 1)u(\nabla_\psi^{-it}\otimes 1).\qedhere
\end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
Let $\beta\,:\,H\curvearrowright B$ be any ergodic $\psi$-preserving action of the CQG $H$ on the finite dimensional C*-algebra $B$. It follows from statement $(b)$ of Proposition \ref{PropQAut} that if $H$ is Kac then $\psi$ is tracial. Moreover, if $\beta$ is a faithful action and $\psi$ is tracial then $H$ is Kac.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{PropUcpSection}
For all $1\leq\kappa\leq K$, the following holds.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $({\rm id}\otimes h)\beta_\kappa=\psi(\cdot)1_\kappa$. In particular, $\beta_\kappa$ is a faithful homomorphism.
\item For all $t\in\mathbb{R}$, $(\sigma_{-t}^{\psi_\kappa}\otimes\sigma_t^h)\beta_\kappa=\beta_\kappa\sigma_t^\psi$  and $(\sigma_{-t}^{\psi_\kappa}\otimes\tau_t^h)\beta_\kappa=\beta_\kappa\sigma_{-t}^\psi$.
\item There exists a unique ucp map $E_\kappa\,:\, M_{N_\kappa}(\mathbb{C})\otimes{\rm L}^\infty(H)\rightarrow B$ such that
$$\psi\circ E_\kappa=\psi_\kappa^{-1}\otimes h\quad\text{and}\quad E_\kappa\circ\beta_\kappa={\rm id}_B.$$
Moreover, $E_\kappa$ is normal, faithful and, for all $1\leq r,s\leq N_\kappa$ and all $a\in{\rm L}^\infty(H)$,
$$E_\kappa(b^\kappa_{rs}\otimes a)=\frac{1}{\delta\lambda^2_{\kappa,s}}\sum_{\gamma,k,l}h\left(\left(u^{rs,\kappa}_{kl,\gamma}\right)^*a\right)b^\gamma_{kl}.$$
In particular, $E_\kappa(e^\kappa_{rs}\otimes 1)=\frac{\delta_{rs}}{\delta\lambda_{\kappa,r}}1_B$.

\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
$(1)$. The unique $\beta$-invariant state $\psi$ is defined by $({\rm id}\otimes h)\beta=\psi(\cdot)1$. Applying $\chi_\kappa$ gives $(1)$. Since $\psi$ is faithful, the maps $\beta_\kappa$ also are.

\vspace{0.2cm}

\noindent$(2)$. Follows from Assertion $(2.b)$ and $(2.c)$ in Proposition \ref{PropQAut}.

\vspace{0.2cm}

\noindent$(3)$. Since $\sigma_t^{\psi_\kappa^{-1}}=\sigma_{-t}^{\psi_\kappa}$ it follows from $(2)$ that the subalgebra $\beta_\kappa(B)\subset M_{N_\kappa}(\mathbb{C})\otimes {\rm L}^\infty(H)$ is globally invariant under the modular group of $\psi_\kappa^{-1}\otimes h$. By Takesaki's Theorem there exists a unique $\psi_\kappa^{-1}\otimes h$-preserving conditional expectation $\mathbb{E}_\kappa\,:\,M_{N_\kappa}(\mathbb{C})\otimes{\rm L}^\infty(H)\rightarrow\beta_\kappa(B)$, which is normal and faithful. Then, $E_\kappa:=\beta_\kappa^{-1}\circ \mathbb{E}_\kappa$ satisfies $E_\kappa\circ\beta_\kappa={\rm id}_B$ and, using $(1)$ and the fact that $\mathbb{E}_\kappa$ is state preserving, we deduce that $\psi\circ E_\kappa=\psi_\kappa^{-1}\otimes h$. From this property and since $\psi_\kappa^{-1}\otimes h$ is faithful, we deduce that $E_\kappa$ is faithful. By $(1)$, $(\beta_\kappa(b^\gamma_{kl}))_{\gamma,k,l}$ is a $\psi_\kappa^{-1}\otimes h$-orthonormal basis of the finite dimensional subalgebra $\beta_\kappa(B)$ which easily implies that
$$\mathbb{E}_\kappa(X)=\sum_{\gamma,k,l}(\psi_\kappa^{-1}\otimes h)(\beta_\kappa(b^\gamma_{kl})^*X)\beta_\kappa(b^\gamma_{kl})\text{ for all }X\in M_{N_\kappa}(\mathbb{C})\otimes{\rm L}^\infty(H).$$
Using the formulas $(b^\gamma_{kl})^*=\left(\frac{\lambda_{\gamma,k}}{\lambda_{\gamma,l}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}b^\gamma_{lk}$ and $b^\kappa_{ip}b^\kappa_{qj}=\lambda_{\kappa,p}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\delta_{pq}b^\kappa_{ij}$ we get:
$$\beta_\kappa(b^\gamma_{kl})^*(b^\kappa_{rs}\otimes a)=\left(\frac{\lambda_{\gamma,k}}{\lambda_{\gamma,l}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\kappa,r}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\sum_ib^\kappa_{is}\otimes u^{ir,\kappa}_{lk,\gamma}a.$$
Since $\psi_\kappa^{-1}(b^\kappa_{is})={\rm Tr}(Q_\kappa^{-1})^{-1}\lambda_{\kappa,s}^{-\frac{3}{2}}\delta_{is}$  and $\left(u^{rs,\kappa}_{kl,\gamma}\right)^*=\left(\frac{\lambda_{\kappa,s}\lambda_{\gamma,k}}{\lambda_{\kappa,r}\lambda_{\gamma,l}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}u^{sr,\kappa}_{lk,\gamma}$ we deduce that:
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}_\kappa(b^\kappa_{rs}\otimes a)&=\sum_{\gamma,k,l}(\psi_\kappa^{-1}\otimes h)(\beta_\kappa(b^\gamma_{kl})^*(b^\kappa_{rs}\otimes a))\beta_\kappa(b^\gamma_{kl})\\
&={\rm Tr}(Q_\kappa^{-1})^{-1}\lambda_{\kappa,r}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\kappa,s}^{-\frac{3}{2}}\sum_{\gamma,k,l}\left(\frac{\lambda_{\gamma,k}}{\lambda_{\gamma,l}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}h(u^{sr,\kappa}_{lk,\gamma}a)\beta_\kappa(b^\gamma_{kl})\\
&={\rm Tr}(Q_\kappa^{-1})^{-1}\lambda_{\kappa,s}^{-2}\sum_{\gamma,k,l}h\left(\left(u^{rs,\kappa}_{kl,\gamma}\right)^*a\right)\beta_\kappa(b^\gamma_{kl}).
\qedhere
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
We will use the same symbol to denote the restriction $$E_\kappa\,:\,M_{N_\kappa}(\mathbb{C})\otimes C_r(H)\rightarrow B$$ which is still ucp and faithful, as well as $E_\kappa:=E_\kappa\circ({\rm id}\otimes\lambda_{H})\,:\,M_{N_\kappa}(\mathbb{C})\otimes C(H)\rightarrow B$, still ucp but not even GNS-faithful if $H$ is not coamenable. Those maps satisfy the same algebraic properties as the initial map.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{LemE} The following holds.
\begin{enumerate}
\item For all $x\in {\rm Pol}(H)$, $1\leq\kappa,\zeta,\gamma\leq K$, $1\leq i,j\leq N_\kappa$, $1\leq k,l\leq N_\gamma$, $1\leq r,p\leq N_\zeta$,
$$\sum_q\lambda_{\gamma,q}^{-1/2}u^{pr,\zeta}_{kq,\gamma}h(u^{ij,\kappa}_{ql,\gamma}x)=\sum_{s,(1),(2)}\lambda_{\zeta,r}^{-1/2}h(u^{ij,\kappa}_{rs,\zeta}x_{(1)})u^{ps,\zeta}_{kl,\gamma}x_{(2)}$$.
\item For all $X=\sum_{ij}b^\kappa_{ij}\otimes x_{ij}\in M_{N_\kappa}(\mathbb{C})\otimes {\rm Pol}(H)$ if $E_\kappa(X)=0$ then
$$\sum_{i,j,(1),(2)}\lambda_{\kappa,i}^{-1/2}\lambda_{\kappa,j}^{-3/2}h(u^{ji,\kappa}_{kl,\gamma}(x_{ij})_{(1)})(x_{ij})_{(2)}=0,\quad\text{for all }\gamma,k,l.$$
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
$(1)$. Fix $x\in {\rm Pol}(H)$, $1\leq\kappa,\zeta,\gamma \leq K$, $1\leq i,j\leq N_\kappa$, $1\leq k,l\leq N_\gamma$ and $1\leq p,r\leq N_\zeta$ and define $Z:=\sum_q\lambda_{\gamma,q}^{-1/2}(1\otimes u^{pr,\zeta}_{kq,\gamma})\Delta(u^{ij,\kappa}_{ql,\gamma}x)$. Using the relation
$$\Delta(u^{ij,\kappa}_{ql,\gamma}x)=\sum_{\zeta',r',s}u^{ij,\kappa}_{r's,\zeta'}x_{(1)}\otimes u^{r's,\zeta'}_{ql,\gamma}x_{(2)},\,\text{we get:}$$
\begin{eqnarray*}
Z&=&\sum_{\zeta',r',s}u^{ij,\kappa}_{r's,\zeta'}x_{(1)}\otimes\left(\sum_q\lambda_{\gamma,q}^{-1/2}u^{pr,\zeta}_{kq,\gamma}u^{r's,\zeta'}_{ql,\gamma}x_{(2)}\right)
=\sum_s\lambda_{\zeta,r}^{-1/2}u^{ij,\kappa}_{rs,\zeta}x_{(1)}\otimes u^{ps,\zeta}_{kl,\gamma}x_{(2)}
\end{eqnarray*}
Hence, using invariance of the Haar state, and the previous equation we get:
\begin{eqnarray*}
(h\otimes{\rm id})(Z)&=&\sum_q\lambda_{\gamma,q}^{-1/2}u^{pr,\zeta}_{kq,\gamma}(h\otimes{\rm id})\Delta(u^{ij,\kappa}_{ql,\gamma}x)=\sum_q\lambda_{\gamma,q}^{-1/2}u^{pr,\zeta}_{kq,\gamma}h(u^{ij,\kappa}_{ql,\gamma}x)\\
&=&\sum_s\lambda_{\zeta,r}^{-1/2}h(u^{ij,\kappa}_{rs,\zeta}x_{(1)})u^{ps,\zeta}_{kl,\gamma}x_{(2)}.
\end{eqnarray*}

\vspace{0.2cm}

\noindent$(2)$. Using the formula in Proposition \ref{PropUcpSection}, we get:
$$0=E_\kappa(X)=\delta^{-1}\sum_{\gamma,k,l}\left(\frac{\lambda_{\gamma,l}}{\lambda_{\gamma,k}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(\sum_{i,j}\lambda_{\kappa,i}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\kappa,j}^{-\frac{3}{2}}h(u^{ji,\kappa}_{kl,\gamma}x_{ij})\right)b^\gamma_{lk}.$$
Hence, for all $\gamma,k,l$ we have $\sum_{i,j}\lambda_{\kappa,i}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\kappa,j}^{-\frac{3}{2}}h(u^{ji,\kappa}_{kl,\gamma}x_{ij})=0$. Using $(1)$ we find, for all $\gamma,\zeta,k,p$,
\begin{eqnarray*}
0&=&\sum_q\lambda_{\gamma,q}^{-1/2}u^{pr,\zeta}_{kq,\gamma}\left(\sum_{i,j}\lambda_{\kappa,i}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\kappa,j}^{-\frac{3}{2}}h(u^{ji,\kappa}_{qk,\gamma}x_{ij})\right)
=\sum_{i,j}\lambda_{\kappa,i}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\kappa,j}^{-\frac{3}{2}}\left(\sum_q\lambda_{\gamma,q}^{-1/2}u^{pr,\zeta}_{kq,\gamma}h(u^{ji,\kappa}_{qk,\gamma}x_{ij})\right)\\
&=&\sum_{i,j}\lambda_{\kappa,i}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\kappa,j}^{-\frac{3}{2}}\left(\sum_{s,(1),(2)}\lambda_{\zeta,r}^{-1/2}h(u^{ij,\kappa}_{rs,\zeta}(x_{ij})_{(1)})u^{ps,\zeta}_{kk,\gamma}(x_{ij})_{(2)}\right).
\end{eqnarray*}
Multiplying by $\lambda_{\gamma,k}^{1/2}$ and summing over $k,\gamma$ we get:
\begin{eqnarray*}
0&=&\sum_k\lambda_{\gamma,k}^{1/2}\left(\sum_{i,j}\lambda_{\kappa,i}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\kappa,j}^{-\frac{3}{2}}\left(\sum_{s,(1),(2)}\lambda_{\zeta,r}^{-1/2}h(u^{ij,\kappa}_{rs,\zeta}(x_{ij})_{(1)})u^{ps,\zeta}_{kk,\gamma}(x_{ij})_{(2)}\right)\right)\\
&=&\sum_{i,j}\lambda_{\kappa,i}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\kappa,j}^{-\frac{3}{2}}\left(\sum_{s,(1),(2)}\lambda_{\zeta,r}^{-1/2}h(u^{ij,\kappa}_{rs,\zeta}(x_{ij})_{(1)})\left(\sum_k\lambda_{\gamma,k}^{1/2}u^{ps,\zeta}_{kk,\gamma}\right)(x_{ij})_{(2)}\right)\\
&=&\left(\frac{\lambda_{\zeta,p}}{\lambda_{\zeta,r}}\right)^{1/2}\sum_{i,j,(1),(2)}\lambda_{\kappa,i}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\kappa,j}^{-\frac{3}{2}}h(u^{ij,\kappa}_{rp,\zeta}(x_{ij})_{(1)})(x_{ij})_{(2)}.
\end{eqnarray*}
This concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{2-ergodic}
A $\psi$-preserving action $\beta\,:\, B\rightarrow B\otimes C(H)$ with associated unitary $u\in\mathcal{L}(B)\otimes C(H)$ is called $2$-\textit{ergodic} if ${\rm dim}({\rm Mor}(u,u))=2$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
Note that if $\beta$ is $2$-ergodic then ${\rm dim}(B)\geq 2$. Moreover, the following holds.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\beta$ is $2$-ergodic if and only if $\mathrm{Mor}(u,u)=\mathbb{C}\eta\eta^\star\oplus\mathbb{C}({\rm id}_B-\eta\eta^\star)$. Indeed, the two vectors $\eta\eta^\star,{\rm id}_B-\eta\eta^\star\in\mathrm{Mor}(u,u)$ are linearly independent whenever ${\rm dim}(B)\geq 2$.
    \item As in $(1)$, we see that $\beta$ is $2$-ergodic if and only if $\mathrm{Mor}(1,u\otimes u) = \mathbb{C} \eta\otimes \eta\oplus \mathbb{C} m^\star\eta$.
    \item A $2$-ergodic action $\beta$ is ergodic. Indeed, if ${\rm dim}({\rm Mor}(u,u))=2$ then $u$ is isomorphic to the sum of two non equivalent irreducible representations which implies that ${\rm dim}(1,u)\leq 1$. Since $\eta\in{\rm Mor}(1,u)$, $\beta$ is ergodic.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ExAction1} The following holds.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The canonical $\psi$-preserving action of ${\rm Aut}^+(B,\psi)$ on $B$ (${\rm dim}(B)\geq 2$) is $2$-ergodic if and only if $\psi$ is a $\delta$-form, in particular the action of $S_N^+$ on $\mathbb{C}^N$ for any $N\geq 2$ is $2$-ergodic. Similarly, the action of $S_N$ on $\mathbb{C}^N$ is also $2$-ergodic for any $N\geq 2$.
    \item  For a finite group $\Lambda$, the action $\widehat{\Lambda}\curvearrowright C^*(\Lambda)$ given by the comultiplication is ergodic and $\tau_\Lambda$-preserving, where $\tau_\Lambda\in C^*(\Lambda)^*$ is the canonical (faithful) trace. This action is not $2$-ergodic whenever $\vert\Lambda\vert\neq 2$ since the corresponding representation $u$ is such that ${\rm dim}(\mathrm{Mor}(\varepsilon,u\otimes u))=\vert \Lambda \vert$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{LemmaHaarProduct}
If $\beta$ is $2$-ergodic then the following holds.
\begin{eqnarray*}
h(u^{ij,\alpha}_{kl,\gamma}u^{rs,\kappa}_{vw,\zeta})&=&\dfrac{\delta}{\delta-1}\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}\delta_{rs}\delta_{vw} (\lambda_{\alpha,i}\lambda_{\gamma,k}\lambda_{\kappa,r}\lambda_{\zeta,v})^{\frac{1}{2}}+\frac{\delta_{\alpha \kappa}\delta_{jr}\delta_{is}\delta_{\gamma \zeta}\delta_{kw}\delta_{lv}}{\delta-1} \left(\frac{\lambda_{\alpha,i}\lambda_{\gamma,k}}{\lambda_{\alpha,j}\lambda_{\gamma,l}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\
  &-& \delta_{ij}\delta_{rs}\delta_{\gamma \zeta}\delta_{kw}\delta_{lv}\frac{1}{\delta-1}\lambda_{\alpha,i}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\kappa,r}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\gamma,k}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\gamma,l}^{-\frac{1}{2}}
  -  \delta_{\alpha \kappa}\delta_{is}\delta_{jr}\delta_{kl}\delta_{vw} \frac{1}{\delta-1}\lambda_{\alpha,j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\alpha,i}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\gamma,k}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\zeta,v}^{\frac{1}{2}}.
\end{eqnarray*}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The action $\beta$ being $2$-ergodic, it is ergodic so its unique invariant state $\psi$ is a $\delta$-form. Moreover, $({\rm id}\otimes h)(u\otimes u)$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathrm{Mor}(1,u\otimes u) = \mathbb{C} \eta\otimes \eta\oplus \mathbb{C} m^\star\eta$. Write $\eta=\sum_{\kappa,i}\lambda_{\kappa,i}^{\frac{1}{2}}b^\kappa_{ii}$, $m^\star\eta = \sum_{\kappa,i,t}\lambda_{\kappa,i}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\kappa,t}^{-\frac{1}{2}} b^\kappa_{it}\otimes b^\kappa_{ti}$, and therefore $\Vert m^\star\eta \Vert^2 = \sum_\kappa {\rm Tr}(Q_\kappa^{-1}){\rm Tr}(Q_\kappa)= \sum_\kappa \delta {\rm Tr}(Q_\kappa) = \delta$, because $\psi$ is a $\delta$-form.
Since $(\eta^\star\otimes \eta^\star) m^\star\eta = 1$ we have $\Vert m^\star\eta - \eta \otimes \eta \Vert^2 = \Vert m^\star\eta \Vert^2-1 =: \delta-1 $. The orthogonal projection on the space is then the orthogonal projection that we obtain taking $(\eta\otimes \eta, \frac{1}{\sqrt{\delta-1}}(m^\star\eta - \eta\otimes \eta))$ as an orthogonal base. The projection is therefore given by $p = \eta\eta^\star\otimes \eta\eta^\star + \frac{1}{\delta-1}(m^\star\eta  - \eta\otimes \eta)(m^\star\eta  - \eta\otimes \eta)^\star$. Note that:
$$
            p = \left(1+\dfrac{1}{\delta-1}\right) (\eta\eta^\star\otimes \eta\eta^\star )+ \frac{1}{\delta-1} m^\star\eta \eta^\star m - \frac{1}{\delta-1}(\eta\otimes \eta)\eta^\star m  - \frac{1}{\delta-1}m^\star \eta (\eta^\star\otimes \eta^\star).$$
            We have:
\begin{eqnarray*}
    \eta\eta^\star\otimes \eta\eta^\star = \sum_{\substack{\alpha,i\\ \gamma,k}} \sum_{\substack{\kappa,r\\ \zeta,v}} (b_{ii}^\alpha \otimes b_{rr}^\kappa)\circ (b_{kk}^\gamma \otimes b_{vv}^\zeta)^\star  (\lambda_{\alpha,i}\lambda_{\gamma,k}\lambda_{\kappa,r}\lambda_{\zeta,v})^{\frac{1}{2}}\\
    m^\star\eta \eta^\star m = \sum_{\substack{\alpha,i,x\\ \gamma,k,y}} (b_{ix}^\alpha \otimes b_{xi}^\alpha)\circ (b_{ky}^\gamma \otimes b_{yk}^\gamma)^\star (\lambda_{\alpha,i}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\alpha,x}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\gamma,k}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\gamma,y}^{-\frac{1}{2}})\\
    (\eta\otimes \eta)\eta^\star m = \sum_{\substack{\alpha,i\\ \kappa,r}} \sum_{\substack{\gamma,k,t}} (b_{ii}^\alpha \otimes b_{rr}^\kappa)\circ (b_{kt}^\gamma \otimes b_{tk}^\gamma)^\star \lambda_{\alpha,i}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\kappa,r}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\gamma,k}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\gamma,t}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\\
    m^\star \eta (\eta^\star\otimes \eta^\star)= \sum_{\substack{\alpha,i,t}} \sum_{\substack{\gamma,k\\ \zeta,v}} (b_{it}^\alpha \otimes b_{ti}^\alpha)\circ (b_{kk}^\gamma \otimes b_{vv}^\zeta)^\star \lambda_{\alpha,t}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\alpha,i}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\gamma,k}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\zeta,v}^{\frac{1}{2}}\\
\end{eqnarray*}
We deduce that the coefficient associated to $(b_{ij}^\alpha \otimes b_{rs}^\kappa)\circ (b_{kl}^\gamma \otimes b_{vw}^\zeta)^\star$ is:
\begin{eqnarray*}
  &\left(1+\dfrac{1}{\delta-1}\right)\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}\delta_{rs}\delta_{vw} (\lambda_{\alpha,i}\lambda_{\gamma,k}\lambda_{\kappa,r}\lambda_{\zeta,v})^{\frac{1}{2}}
  + \delta_{\alpha \kappa}\delta_{jr}\delta_{is}\delta_{\gamma \zeta}\delta_{kw}\delta_{lv}\frac{1}{\delta-1} (\lambda_{\alpha,i}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\alpha,j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\gamma,k}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\gamma,l}^{-\frac{1}{2}})\\
  &- \delta_{ij}\delta_{rs}\delta_{\gamma \zeta}\delta_{kw}\delta_{lv}\frac{1}{\delta-1}\lambda_{\alpha,i}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\kappa,r}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\gamma,k}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\gamma,l}^{-\frac{1}{2}}
  -  \delta_{\alpha \kappa}\delta_{is}\delta_{jr}\delta_{kl}\delta_{vw} \frac{1}{\delta-1}\lambda_{\alpha,j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\alpha,i}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\gamma,k}^{\frac{1}{2}}\lambda_{\zeta,v}^{\frac{1}{2}}.
\end{eqnarray*}
This coefficient is equal to $h(u^{ij,\alpha}_{kl,\gamma}u^{rs,\kappa}_{vw,\zeta}).$
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{LemmaT}
If $\beta$ is $2$-ergodic, $\kappa$ is such that $N_\kappa\geq 2$ then, for any unital C*-algebra $C$,
\begin{enumerate}
    \item If $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and $u\in\mathcal{U}(B\otimes C)$ are such that $\sigma_{-t}^{\psi_\kappa}\otimes\sigma^h_t\otimes{\rm id}_C={\rm Ad}((\beta_\kappa\otimes{\rm id})(u))$ then $u\in\mathbb{C}1\otimes\mathcal{Z}(C)$ and $\sigma_t^h={\rm id}$.
    \item $\{u\in\mathcal{U}(B\otimes C)\,:\,{\rm Ad}((\beta_\kappa\otimes{\rm id})(u))={\rm id}\}\subset\mathbb{C}1_B\otimes\mathcal{Z}(C)$.
        
    \item If $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and $u\in\mathcal{U}(B\otimes C)$ are such that $\sigma_{-t}^{\psi_\kappa}\otimes\tau^H_t\otimes{\rm id}_C={\rm Ad}((\beta_\kappa\otimes{\rm id})(u))$ then $u\in\mathbb{C}1\otimes\mathcal{Z}(C)$ and $\tau^H_t={\rm id}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
$(1)$. Let $t\in\mathbb{R}$ and $u\in\mathcal{U}(B\otimes C)$ be such that $\sigma_{-t}^{\psi_\kappa}\otimes\sigma^h_t\otimes{\rm id}_C={\rm Ad}((\beta_\kappa\otimes{\rm id})(u))$. Recall that $\sigma_t^\psi={\rm Ad}(b_t)$, where $b_t=\sum_{\gamma,r}\lambda_{\gamma,r}^{it}e^\gamma_{rr}=\sum_{\gamma,r}\lambda_{\gamma,r}^{it+1/2}b^\gamma_{rr}\in B$ is unitary and $b_t^*=b_{-t}$. Then, for all $b\in B$ and $c\in C$,
\begin{eqnarray*}
(\sigma_{-t}^{\psi_\kappa}\otimes\sigma^h_t\otimes{\rm id}_C)(\beta_\kappa\otimes{\rm id})(b\otimes c)&=&\beta_\kappa(\sigma_t^\psi(b))\otimes c=\beta_\kappa(b_tbb_{-t})\otimes c\\
&=&(\beta_\kappa\otimes{\rm id})((b_t\otimes 1)(b\otimes c)(b_{-t}\otimes 1))\\
&=&(\beta_\kappa\otimes{\rm id})(u)(\beta_\kappa\otimes{\rm id})(b\otimes c)(\beta_\kappa\otimes{\rm id})(u^*)\\
&=&(\beta_\kappa\otimes{\rm id})(u(b\otimes c)u^*).
\end{eqnarray*}
Since $\beta_\kappa$ is faithful, we deduce that $(b_t\otimes 1)(b\otimes c)(b_{-t}\otimes 1)=u(b\otimes c)u^*$ for all $b\in B$, $c\in C$. Hence, $v:=(b_{-t}\otimes 1)u\in\mathcal{Z}(B\otimes C)$. Since $v$ is unitary and central in $B\otimes C$, we may write $v=\sum_{\gamma,r}e^\gamma_{rr}\otimes\alpha_\gamma=\sum\lambda_{\gamma,r}^{1/2} b^\gamma_{rr}\otimes\alpha_\gamma$ where $\alpha_\gamma\in \mathcal{U}(\mathcal{Z}(C))$. Then, $u=(b_t\otimes 1)v=\sum_{\gamma,r}\lambda_{\gamma,r}^{it+1/2} b^\gamma_{rr}\otimes \alpha_\gamma$ and $u^*=\sum_{\zeta,s}\lambda_{\zeta,s}^{-it+1/2}b^\zeta_{ss}\otimes \alpha^*_\zeta $. It follows that:
$$(\beta_\kappa\otimes{\rm id})(u)=\sum_{\gamma,r,k,t}\lambda_{\gamma,r}^{it+1/2} b^\kappa_{kt}\otimes u^{kt,\kappa}_{rr,\gamma}\otimes \alpha_\gamma\,\,\text{and}\,\,(\beta_\kappa\otimes{\rm id})(u^*)=\sum_{\zeta,s,t',l}\lambda_{\zeta,s}^{-it+1/2} b^\kappa_{t'l}\otimes u^{t'l,\kappa}_{ss,\zeta}\otimes \alpha_\zeta^*.$$
Fix $1\leq p\leq N_\kappa$. Using the formula $b^\kappa_{kt}b^\kappa_{pp}b^\kappa_{t'l}=\frac{\delta_{tp}\delta_{t'p}}{\lambda_{\kappa,p}}b^\kappa_{kl}$, we find:
$$
(\beta_\kappa\otimes{\rm id})(u)(b^\kappa_{pp}\otimes 1\otimes 1)(\beta_\kappa\otimes{\rm id})(u^*)=\sum_{\gamma,\zeta,r,s,k,l}\left(\frac{\lambda_{\gamma,r}}{\lambda_{\zeta,s}}\right)^{it}\frac{(\lambda_{\gamma,r}\lambda_{\zeta,s})^{1/2}}{\lambda_{\kappa,p}}b^\kappa_{kl}\otimes u^{kp,\kappa}_{rr,\gamma}u^{pl,\kappa}_{ss,\zeta}\otimes \alpha_\gamma\alpha_{\zeta}^*.
$$
Note that $(\sigma_{-t}^{\psi_\kappa}\otimes\sigma_t^h\otimes{\rm id}_C)(b^\kappa_{pp}\otimes 1\otimes 1)=b^\kappa_{pp}\otimes 1\otimes 1$ hence,
\begin{equation}\label{EqT}\sum_{\gamma,\zeta,r,s}\left(\frac{\lambda_{\gamma,r}}{\lambda_{\zeta,s}}\right)^{it}\frac{(\lambda_{\gamma,r}\lambda_{\zeta,s})^{1/2}}{\lambda_{\kappa,p}} u^{pp,\kappa}_{rr,\gamma}u^{pp,\kappa}_{ss,\zeta}\otimes \alpha_\gamma\alpha_{\zeta}^*=1\otimes 1.\end{equation}
By the Haar state formula given in Lemma \ref{LemmaHaarProduct} we have:
$$h(u^{pp,\kappa}_{rr,\gamma}u^{pp,\kappa}_{ss,\zeta})=\left(\frac{\delta}{\delta-1}\lambda_{\kappa,p}-\frac{1}{\delta-1}\right)(\lambda_{\gamma,r}\lambda_{\zeta,s})^{1/2}+\delta_{\gamma,\zeta}\delta_{rs}\frac{1-\lambda_{\kappa,p}}{\delta-1}.$$
Applying $h\otimes{\rm id}_C$ to Equation $(\ref{EqT})$ we get:
$$
\left(\frac{\delta}{\delta-1}-\frac{1}{\delta-1}\lambda_{\kappa,p}^{-1}\right)\left[\sum_{\gamma,\zeta,r,s}\left(\frac{\lambda_{\gamma,r}}{\lambda_{\zeta,s}}\right)^{it}\lambda_{\gamma,r}\lambda_{\zeta,s}\alpha_\gamma\alpha_{\zeta}^*\right]+\left(\frac{1}{\delta-1}\lambda_{\kappa,p}^{-1}-\frac{1}{\delta-1}\right)1=1.
$$
Define $w:=\sum_{\gamma,r}\lambda_{\gamma,r}\lambda_{\gamma,r}^{it}\alpha_\gamma\in \mathcal{Z}(C)$. Note that, since $N_\kappa\geq 2$, $\delta=\sum_{t}\lambda_{\kappa,t}^{-1}>\lambda_{\kappa,p}^{-1}$ hence,
$$\left(\frac{\delta}{\delta-1}-\frac{1}{\delta-1}\lambda_{\kappa,p}^{-1}\right)\neq 0$$
and $ww^*=\sum_{\gamma,\zeta,r,s}\left(\frac{\lambda_{\gamma,r}}{\lambda_{\zeta,s}}\right)^{it}\lambda_{\gamma,r}\lambda_{\zeta,s}\alpha_\gamma\alpha_{\zeta}^*=1$. We conclude that $w$ is unitary so the convex combination $w=\sum_{\gamma,r}\lambda_{\gamma,r}\lambda_{\gamma,r}^{it}\alpha_\gamma$ is an extreme point in the unit ball of $C$ which implies that $\lambda_{\gamma,r}^{it}\alpha_\gamma=\lambda_{\zeta,s}^{it}\alpha_\zeta$ for all $\gamma,\zeta,r,s$.
Writing $a\in\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{Z}(C))$ the unitary satisfying $a=\lambda_{\gamma,r}^{it}\alpha_\gamma$ for all $1\leq\gamma\leq K$ and all $1\leq r\leq N_\gamma$ one has $$u=\sum_{\gamma,r}\lambda_{\gamma,r}^{it+1/2} b^\gamma_{rr}\otimes \alpha_\gamma=\sum\lambda_{\gamma,r}^{1/2}b^\gamma_{rr}\otimes a=1\otimes a.$$ Hence, for all $x\in{\rm L}^\infty(H)$, one has:
\begin{eqnarray*}
1\otimes\sigma_t^h(x)\otimes 1&=&(\sigma_{-t}^{\psi_\kappa}\otimes\sigma_t^h\otimes{\rm id})(1\otimes x\otimes 1)={\rm Ad}((\beta_\kappa\otimes{\rm id})(u))(1\otimes x\otimes 1)\\
&=&(1\otimes x\otimes aa^*)
=1\otimes x\otimes 1.
\end{eqnarray*}
It follows that $\sigma_t^h={\rm id}$.

\vspace{0.2cm}

\noindent$(2)$ follows from $(1)$ (with $t=0$).
\vspace{0.2cm}

\noindent$(3)$ can be obtained through the same reasoning as for $(1)$, replacing the modular group relation $(\sigma_{-t}^{\psi_\kappa}\otimes \sigma_t^h)\beta_\kappa = \beta_\kappa\circ \sigma_t^\psi$ by the scaling group relation $(\sigma_{-t}^{\psi_\kappa}\otimes \tau_t^H)\beta_\kappa = \beta_\kappa\circ \sigma_{-t}^\psi$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{LemmaTdim1}
If $\beta$ is $2$-ergodic and $N_\kappa=1$ for all $\kappa$ (so that $B=\mathbb{C}^K$) and $K\geq 3$ then, for any unital C*-algebra $C$ and any $1\leq \gamma,\kappa\leq K$ with $\kappa\neq\gamma$,
$$\mathbb{C}1\otimes C=\beta_\gamma(\mathbb{C}^K)\otimes C\cap\beta_\kappa(\mathbb{C}^K)\otimes C\subset C(H)\otimes C.$$
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Since $\beta$ is ergodic, $\psi$ is a $\delta$-form. It is easy to check that the unique $\delta$-form on $\mathbb{C}^K$ is the uniform normalized trace and $\delta=K$. Write $u=\sum_{i,j=1}^Ke_{ij}\otimes u_{ij}$, where $e_{ij}$ are the canonical matrix units, the unitary representation of $H$ associated with $\beta$. Note that $\beta_i(\mathbb{C}^K)={\rm Span}\{u_{ij}\,:\,1\leq j\leq K\}$. By Lemma \ref{LemmaHaarProduct} and since $\delta=K$ we find:

\begin{eqnarray*}
h(u_{ij} u_{kl}) &=& \dfrac{1}{K(K-1)} +\dfrac{1}{K-1}\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl} - \dfrac{1}{K(K-1)}\delta_{jl} -  \dfrac{1}{K(K-1)}\delta_{ik}\\
  &=& \begin{cases}
    \dfrac{1}{K} & \text{if $i=k$ and $j=l$}.\\
    0 & \text{if $i=k$ and $j\neq l$, or $i\neq k$ and $j= l$}.\\
    \dfrac{1}{K(K-1)} & \text{otherwise}.\\
  \end{cases}
\end{eqnarray*} 
Let $E_i\,:\,{\rm L}^\infty(H)\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^K$ be the ucp map from Proposition \ref{PropUcpSection}. Using the formula above for the Haar state as well as the formula given in Proposition \ref{PropUcpSection} we obtain:
$$E_i(u_{jk})=\left\{\begin{array}{lcl}\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{l\neq k}e_{l}&\text{if}& i\neq j,\\e_k&\text{if}&i=j.\end{array}\right.$$
Let $i\neq j$ and $w\in \beta_i(\mathbb{C}^K)\otimes C\cap \beta_j(\mathbb{C}^K)\otimes C$ be a unitary ($i\neq j$), then we can write $$w  = \sum_k u_{jk}\otimes \mu_k = \sum_l u_{il}\otimes \nu_l\text{ where, for all }k,l,\,\,\mu_k,\nu_l\in\mathcal{U}(C).$$ Applying $E_i\otimes{\rm id}_C$ to $w$, we get that for any $l$, $ \nu_l = \frac{1}{K-1} \sum_{k\neq l} \mu_k$. In particular, $\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{k\neq l} \mu_k$ is a unitary so it is an extreme point in the unit ball of $C$. It follows that $\mu_k=\mu_{k'}$ for all $k,k'\neq l$. Since this holds for all $l$ and $K\geq 3$, we deduce that $\mu_k$ does not depend on $k$ hence $w$ is of the form $w=1\otimes v$, with $v\in\mathcal{U}(C)$. The C*-algebra $\beta_i(\mathbb{C}^K)\otimes C\cap\beta_j(\mathbb{C}^K)\otimes C$ being the linear span of its unitaries, we get $\beta_i(\mathbb{C}^K)\otimes C\cap\beta_j(\mathbb{C}^K)\otimes C=\mathbb{C}1\otimes C$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{PropMotivation}
If $A$ is a unital C*-algebra with unital $*$-homomorphisms $\iota\,:\, C(S_N^+)\rightarrow A$ and $\pi\,:\,C(G)\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^N\otimes A$ such that $[\pi(a),({\rm id}\otimes\iota)(\beta(b))]=0$ for all $a\in C(G)$ and $b\in\mathbb{C}^N$ then, there exists a unique unital $*$-homomorphism $\widetilde{\pi}\,:\,C(G\wr_*S_N^+)\rightarrow A$ such that $$({\rm id}\otimes\widetilde{\pi})\rho=\pi\text{ and }\widetilde{\pi}\vert_{C(S_N^+)}=\iota.$$
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The uniqueness being obvious, let us show the existence. Write $\pi(a)=\sum_ie_i\otimes\pi_i(a)$ and note that, since $\pi$ is a unital $*$-homomorphism, each $\pi_i\,:\, C(G)\rightarrow A$ is a unital $*$-homomorphism. Define $\pi_0\,:\, C(G)^{*N}*C(S_N^+)\rightarrow A$ by $\pi_0\circ\nu_i:=\pi_i$ and $\pi_0\vert_{C(S_N^+)}:=\iota$. Note that the commutations relations $[\pi(a),({\rm id}\otimes\iota)(\beta(b))]=0$ imply that, for all $a\in C(G)$ and all $1\leq i,j\leq N$ one has $\pi_0(\nu_i(a)u_{ij}-u_{ij}\nu_i(a))=0$. Hence $I\subseteq\ker(\pi_0)$ which implies that there exists a unital $*$-homomorphism $\widetilde{\pi}\,:\,C(G\wr_* S_N^+)\rightarrow A$ satisfying the properties of the Proposition.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{RmkIota} Suppose that $C(\mathbb{G})$ exists then $\iota$ and $\rho$ are faithful (in particular, both $\iota_H$ and $\iota_F$ are faithful). Indeed, it follows from the universal property, taking $C=C(H)\otimes_{{\rm max}} C(G)$, $\iota'_H(x)=x\otimes 1_{C(F)}$, $\iota'_F(f)=1_{C(H)}\otimes f$ and $\rho'(a)=1_B\otimes 1_{C(H)}\otimes a$, that there exists a unique unital $*$-homomorphism $\pi\,:\,C(\mathbb{G})\rightarrow C(H)\otimes_{{\rm max}} C(G)$ such that
    $$({\rm id}\otimes\pi)\rho(a)=1_B\otimes 1_{C(H)}\otimes a\text{ for all }a\in C(G)\text{ and }\pi\circ\iota={\rm id}.$$
We easily deduce that $\iota$ and $\rho$ are faithful.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
When $F$ equals $G$ i.e.  the inclusion $C(F)\subset C(G)$ is surjective then $C(\mathbb{G})$ exists: it is easy to see that $C(\mathbb{G}):=C(H\times G)=C(H)\otimes_{{\rm max}} C(G)$ with $\iota_H(x)=x\otimes 1_{C(G)}$, $\iota_F(a)=1_{C(H)}\otimes a$ and $\rho(a)=1_B\otimes 1_{C(H)}\otimes a$ for all $x\in C(H)$ and $a\in C(G)$ satisfy the universal property.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
The following holds.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $B$ is finite dimensional then $C(\mathbb{G})$ exists.
\item If $F$ is trivial, $G$ is non-trivial and $B$ is abelian then $C(\mathbb{G})$ exists if and only if $B$ is finite dimensional.
\item If $C(\mathbb{G})$ exists then $C(\mathbb{G})$ is generated, as a C*-algebra, by 
$$\iota_H(C(H))\cup\{(\omega\otimes{\rm id})(\rho(a))\,:\,a\in C(G) ,\,\omega\in B^*\}.$$
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
$(1)$. If $B$ is finite dimensional, it is known \cite{FMP24} that the universal quantum homomorphism $\rho\,:\, C(G)\rightarrow B\otimes \mathcal{U}$ exists. Then, the C*-algebra
$$C(\mathbb{G}):=\mathcal{U}*(C(H)\otimes_{{\rm max}} C(F))/I,$$
where $I$ is the closed two sided ideal generated by $$\{(\omega\otimes{\rm id})(\rho(a)\beta(b)-\beta(b)\rho(a))\,:\,\omega\in B^*,\,a\in C(G),\,b\in B\}$$
and by $\{(\omega\otimes{\rm id})(\rho(f)-1_B\otimes f)\,:\,\omega\in B^*,\,f\in C(F)\}$ does the job.

\vspace{0.2cm}

\noindent$(2)$. Suppose that $C(\mathbb{G})$ exists and define $\mathcal{U}\subset C(\mathbb{G})$ to be the C*-subalgebra of $C(\mathbb{G})$ generated by $\{(\omega\otimes{\rm id})(\rho(a))\,:\,a\in C(G) ,\,\omega\in B^*\}$ so that $\rho(C(G))\subset B\otimes\mathcal{U}$. We show below that $\rho\,:\, C(G)\rightarrow B\otimes\mathcal{U}$ is the universal quantum homomorphism from $C(G)$ to $B$ in the sense of \cite{FMP24}. Since ${\rm dim}(C(G))\geq 2$ \cite[Theorem D]{FMP24} will imply that $B$ is finite dimensional. Let $\pi\,:\,C(G)\rightarrow B\otimes C$ be a unital $*$-homomorphism and define $\iota'_H:=\varepsilon_H(\cdot)1_C\,:\,C(H)\rightarrow C$. Note that $({\rm id}\otimes\iota'_H)(\beta(b))=b\otimes 1_C$ and since $B$ is abelian we have $[({\rm id}\otimes\iota'_H)(\beta(b)),\pi(a)]=0$ for all $a\in C(G)$ and $b\in B$. It follows that there exists a unique unital $*$-homomorphism $\nu\,:\,C(\mathbb{G})\rightarrow C$ such that $({\rm id}\otimes\nu)\circ\rho=\pi$ (and $\nu\circ\iota_H=\iota'_H$). Defining $\widetilde{\pi}:=\nu\vert_{\mathcal{U}}$ we have $({\rm id}\otimes\widetilde{\pi})\rho=\pi$ and the uniqueness of $\widetilde{\pi}$ is clear.

\vspace{0.2cm}

\noindent$(3)$. It is a direct consequence of the uniqueness in the universal property.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{ThmDefFreeWr}
There exists a unique unital $*$-homomorphism $\Delta\,:\,C(\mathbb{G})\rightarrow C(\mathbb{G})\otimes C(\mathbb{G})$ such that $\Delta\vert_{C(H)\otimes_{{\rm max}} C(F)}=\Delta_{H\times F}$ and $({\rm id}\otimes\Delta)\rho=(\beta_G\otimes{\rm id})({\rm id}\otimes\rho)\Delta_G$. Moreover,
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $(C(\mathbb{G}),\Delta)$ is a CQG and $C(H\times F) = C(H)\otimes_{{\rm max}} C(F) \subset C(\mathbb{G})$ is a dual quantum subgroup.
    \item The counit of $\mathbb{G}$ is the unique character of $C(\mathbb{G})$ satisfying $$({\rm id}\otimes\varepsilon_\mathbb{G})\rho=\varepsilon_G(\cdot)1_B\text{ and }\varepsilon_\mathbb{G}\vert_{C(H\times F)}=\varepsilon_{H\times F}.$$
    \item If $v\in\mathcal{L}(H_v)\otimes C(G)$ is a f.d. unitary representation of $G$ then,
    $$a(v):=({\rm id}\otimes(L_B\otimes{\rm id})\rho)(v)u_{23}\in\mathcal{L}(H_v\otimes B)\otimes C(\mathbb{G})$$
    is a unitary representation of $\mathbb{G}$ on $H_v\otimes B$ and $\overline{a(v)}\simeq a(\overline{v})$.
    \item If $v\in \mathcal{L}(H_v)\otimes C(F)$ is a f.d. representation of $F$, seen as a representation of $G$ by the fact that $\mathrm{Rep}(F)$ is a full subcategory of $\mathrm{Rep}(G)$, then the representation $a(v)$ is the representation $v\otimes u\in \mathcal{L}(H_v\otimes B)\otimes C(H\times F),$ seen as a representation of $C(\mathbb{G})$ because we can see $\mathrm{Rep}(H\times F)$ as a full subcategory of $\mathrm{Rep}(\mathbb{G})$.
    \item Every irreducible representation of $\mathbb{G}$ is equivalent to a subrepresentation of a tensor product of representations of the form $a(v)$, for $v\in{\rm Irr}(G)$, and irreducible representations of $H$. If the action $\beta$ is faithful, any irreducible of $G$ is equivalent to a subrepresentation of a tensor product of $a(v)$, for $v\in{\rm Irr}(G)$.
    \item For all $v,w,t\in\mathrm{Rep}(G)$ and all $S\in\mathrm{Mor}_G(v\otimes w,t)$, the map
    $$(S\otimes m)\Sigma_{23}\,:\,H_v\otimes B\otimes H_w\otimes B\rightarrow H_t\otimes B$$
    is in $\mathrm{Mor}_\mathbb{G}(a(v)\otimes a(w),a(t))$, where $\Sigma_{23}:H_v\otimes B\otimes H_w\otimes B\rightarrow H_v\otimes H_w\otimes B\otimes B$ is the flip map.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Let $\iota':=\Delta_{H\times F}\,:\, C(H\times F)\rightarrow C(\mathbb{G})\otimes C(\mathbb{G})$, from which we get $\iota'_H=\Delta_H$ and $\iota'_F=\Delta_F$ with commuting images and $\rho':=(\beta_G\otimes{\rm id})({\rm id}\otimes\rho)\Delta_G\,:\,C(G)\rightarrow B\otimes C(\mathbb{G})\otimes C(\mathbb{G})$. For $a\in {\rm Pol}(G)$ one has $\rho'(a)=\sum (\beta_G\otimes{\rm id})(a_{(1)}\otimes\rho(a_{(2)}))=\sum(\rho(a_{(1)})\otimes 1)(\beta\otimes{\rm id})(\rho(a_{(2)}))$, where $\Delta_G(a)=\sum a_{(1)}\otimes a_{(2)}$. Hence,
\begin{eqnarray*}
\rho'(a)({\rm id}\otimes\iota'_H)(\beta(b))&=&\rho'(a)({\rm id}\otimes\Delta_{H})(\beta(b))=\rho'(a)(\beta\otimes{\rm id})(\beta(b))\\
&=&\sum(\rho(a_{(1)})\otimes 1)(\beta\otimes{\rm id})(\rho(a_{(2)}))(\beta\otimes{\rm id})(\beta(b))\\
&=&\sum(\rho(a_{(1)})\otimes 1)(\beta\otimes{\rm id})(\rho(a_{(2)})\beta(b))\\
&=&\sum(\rho(a_{(1)})\otimes 1)(\beta\otimes{\rm id})(\beta(b))(\beta\otimes{\rm id})(\rho(a_{(2)}))\\
&=&(\beta\otimes{\rm id})(\beta(b))\sum(\rho(a_{(1)})\otimes 1)(\beta\otimes{\rm id})(\rho(a_{(2)}))\\
&=&({\rm id}\otimes\iota'_H)(\beta(b))\rho'(a).
\end{eqnarray*}

\noindent We also have that for $f\in {\rm Pol}(F)$, $\Delta_G(f)=\Delta_F(f)=\sum f_{(1)}\otimes f_{(2)}\in{\rm Pol}(F)\otimes{\rm Pol}(F)$ and:
\begin{eqnarray*}
\rho'(f) &=&(\beta_G\otimes{\rm id})({\rm id}\otimes\rho)\Delta_G(f)
        = \sum(\beta_G\otimes{\rm id})\left(f_{(1)}\otimes\rho(f_{(2)})\right)\\
        &=&\sum(\beta_G\otimes{\rm id})(f_{(1)}\otimes 1_B\otimes f_{(2)})=\sum\rho(f_{(1)})\otimes f_{(2)}=\sum 1_B\otimes f_{(1)}\otimes f_{(2)}\\
        &=&1_B\otimes\Delta_F(f)=1_B\otimes\iota'_F(f).
\end{eqnarray*}

\noindent The existence of $\Delta\,:\, C(\mathbb{G})\rightarrow C(\mathbb{G})\otimes C(\mathbb{G})$ now follows from the universal property.

\vspace{0.2cm}

\noindent Let us show that $({\rm id}_{\mathcal{L}(H_v\otimes B)}\otimes\Delta)(a(v))=a(v)_{12}a(v)_{13}$ $\forall v\in\mathrm{Rep}(G)$.
\begin{eqnarray*}
&&({\rm id}\otimes\Delta)[({\rm id}\otimes(L_B\otimes{\rm id})\rho)(v)]\\
&=&({\rm id}_{\mathcal{L}(H_v)}\otimes L_B\otimes{\rm id}_{C(\mathbb{G})}\otimes{\rm id}_{C(\mathbb{G})})({\rm id}_{\mathcal{L}(H_v)}\otimes({\rm id}_B\otimes\Delta)\rho)(v)\\
&=&({\rm id}\otimes L_B\otimes{\rm id}\otimes{\rm id})({\rm id}\otimes\beta_G\otimes{\rm id})({\rm id}\otimes{\rm id}\otimes\rho)({\rm id}\otimes\Delta_G)(v)\\
&=&({\rm id}\otimes L_B\otimes{\rm id}\otimes{\rm id})({\rm id}\otimes\beta_G\otimes{\rm id})({\rm id}\otimes{\rm id}\otimes\rho)(v_{12}v_{13})\\
&=&({\rm id}\otimes L_B\otimes{\rm id}\otimes{\rm id})({\rm id}\otimes\beta_G\otimes{\rm id})(v_{12}[({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(v)]_{134})\\
&=&({\rm id}\otimes L_B\otimes{\rm id}\otimes{\rm id})\bigg([({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(v)]_{123}({\rm id}\otimes\beta\otimes{\rm id})(({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(v))\bigg).
\end{eqnarray*}
Since $u$ is a representation of $H$ one has $({\rm id}_{\mathcal{L}(B)}\otimes\Delta)(u)=({\rm id}_{\mathcal{L}(B)}\otimes\Delta_H)(u)=u_{12}u_{13}$ hence,
$$
({\rm id}_{\mathcal{L}(H_v\otimes B)}\otimes\Delta)(a(v))=({\rm id}_{\mathcal{L}(H_v\otimes B)}\otimes\Delta)[({\rm id}\otimes(L_B\otimes{\rm id})\rho)(v)]({\rm id}_{\mathcal{L}(H_v\otimes B)}\otimes\Delta)(u_{23})$$
$$
=({\rm id}\otimes L_B\otimes{\rm id}\otimes{\rm id})\bigg([({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(v)]_{123}({\rm id}\otimes\beta\otimes{\rm id})(({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(v))\bigg)u_{23}u_{24}.$$
\noindent On the other hand, viewing $a(v)_{12}a(v)_{13}$ as a $4$ legged object in $\mathcal{L}(H_v)\otimes\mathcal{L}(B)\otimes C(\mathbb{G})\otimes C(\mathbb{G})$, and using the relation $u(L_B(b)\otimes 1)u^*=(L_B\otimes{\rm id})(\beta(b))$, we get:
\begin{eqnarray*}
&&a(v)_{12}a(v)_{13}\\
&=&({\rm id}\otimes L_B\otimes{\rm id}\otimes{\rm id})\left([({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(v)]_{123}\right)u_{23}({\rm id}\otimes L_B\otimes{\rm id}\otimes{\rm id})\left([({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(v)]_{124}\right)u_{24}\\
&=&({\rm id}\otimes L_B\otimes{\rm id}\otimes{\rm id})\bigg([({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(v)]_{123}({\rm id}\otimes\beta\otimes{\rm id})(({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(v))\bigg)u_{23}u_{24}.
\end{eqnarray*}
This shows that $({\rm id}_{\mathcal{L}(H_v\otimes B)}\otimes\Delta)(a(v))=a(v)_{12}a(v)_{13}$, $\forall v\in\mathrm{Rep}(G)$.

\vspace{0.2cm}

\noindent We now prove $(6)$. Let $v,w\in\mathrm{Rep}(G)$. Viewing $(\Sigma_{23}\otimes 1)a(v)_{13}a(w)_{23}(\Sigma_{23}\otimes 1)$ as a $5$ legged object in $\mathcal{L}(H_v)\otimes\mathcal{L}(H_w)\otimes\mathcal{L}(B)\otimes\mathcal{L}(B)\otimes C(\mathbb{G})$ one has:
$$(\Sigma_{23}\otimes 1)a(v)_{13}a(w)_{23}(\Sigma_{23}\otimes 1)=[({\rm id}\otimes(L_B\otimes{\rm id})\rho)(v)]_{135}u_{35}[({\rm id}\otimes(L_B\otimes{\rm id})\rho)(v)]_{245}u_{45}$$

\noindent Hence, for $a,b\in B$, we get, with $Y:=(\Sigma_{23}\otimes 1)a(v)_{13}a(w)_{23}(1\otimes a\otimes 1\otimes b\otimes 1)$,
\begin{eqnarray*}
Y&=&[({\rm id}\otimes(L_B\otimes{\rm id})\rho)(v)]_{135}u_{35}[({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(v)]_{245}(1\otimes 1\otimes a\otimes\beta(b))\\
&=&[({\rm id}\otimes(L_B\otimes{\rm id})\rho)(v)]_{135}u_{35}(1\otimes 1\otimes a\otimes\beta(b))[({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(v)]_{245}\\
&=&[({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(v)]_{135}\beta(a)_{35}\beta(b)_{45}[({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(v)]_{245}.
\end{eqnarray*}

\noindent It follows that, for any $S\in\mathrm{Mor}_G(v\otimes w,t)$ one has:
\begin{eqnarray*}
(S\otimes m\otimes 1)Y&=&(S\otimes{\rm id}_B\otimes 1)[({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(v)]_{134}(1\otimes1\otimes\beta(a)\beta(b))[({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(w)]_{234}\\
&=&(S\otimes{\rm id}_B\otimes 1)[({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(v)]_{134}[({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(w)]_{234}(1\otimes1\otimes\beta(ab))\\
&=&(S\otimes{\rm id}_B\otimes 1)({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(v_{13}w_{23})(1\otimes1\otimes\beta(ab))\\
&=&({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(t)(S\otimes{\rm id}_B\otimes1)(1\otimes1\otimes\beta(ab))\\
&=&({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(t)(S\otimes{\rm id}_B\otimes1)u_{34}(1\otimes 1\otimes ab\otimes 1)\\
&=&({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(t)u_{23}(S\otimes m\otimes1)(1\otimes 1\otimes a\otimes b\otimes 1)\\
&=&a(t)((S\otimes m)\Sigma_{23})\otimes 1)(1\otimes a\otimes 1\otimes b\otimes 1)
\end{eqnarray*}
\noindent Since this is true for all $a,b\in B$, it follows that
$$((S\otimes m)\Sigma_{23}\otimes 1)a(v)_{13}a(w)_{23}=a(t)((S\otimes m)\Sigma_{23}\otimes 1).$$

\noindent To show that $(C(\mathbb{G}),\Delta)$ is a CQG, we will use the version \cite[Definition 1.1]{FP16} of the definition of a CQG. We already checked the second condition of \cite[Definition 1.1]{FP16}. Let us now check the first condition. Let $\mathcal{X}$ be the set of coefficients of $a(v)$, for $v\in{\rm Irr}(G)$. It suffices to show that the unital $*$-subalgebra of $C(\mathbb{G})$ generated by $\mathcal{X}$ and ${\rm Pol}(H)$ is dense in $C(\mathbb{G})$. For $\omega\in B^*$ define $\omega_0\in\mathcal{L}(B)^*$, $\omega_0(T):=\omega(T1_B)$. Since $u(1_B\otimes1)=1_B\otimes 1$ we have,
\begin{eqnarray*}
({\rm id}\otimes\omega_0\otimes{\rm id})(a(v))&=&({\rm id}\otimes\omega\otimes{\rm id})\left(({\rm id}\otimes(L_B\otimes{\rm id})\rho)(v)u_{23}(1\otimes 1_B\otimes 1)\right)\\
&=&({\rm id}\otimes\omega\otimes{\rm id})\left(({\rm id}\otimes(L_B\otimes{\rm id})\rho)(v)(1\otimes 1_B\otimes 1)\right)\\
&=&({\rm id}\otimes\omega\otimes{\rm id})\left(({\rm id}\otimes\rho)(v)\right)=({\rm id}\otimes(\omega\otimes{\rm id})\rho)(v).
\end{eqnarray*}
It follows that, for any $v\in\mathrm{Rep}(G)$, $(\omega\otimes{\rm id})\rho(v_{ij})\in\mathcal{X}$, for any coefficient $v_{ij}$ of $v$ and any $\omega\in B^*$. Hence, $\{(\omega\otimes{\rm id})\rho(a)\,:\,a\in{\rm Pol}(G),\,\omega\in B^*\}\subset{\rm Span}(\mathcal{X})$. Moreover, since $a(1)=u$, $\mathcal{X}$ also contains the coefficients of $u$. So the $*$-algebra generated by $\mathcal{X}$ is dense in $C(\mathbb{G})$ whenever the action $\beta$ is faithful. In general, the $*$-algebra generated by $\mathcal{X}$ and ${\rm Pol}(H)$ is dense in $C(\mathbb{G})$. It also implies $(5)$, by the general theory of CQG, once we know that $(C(\mathbb{G}),\Delta)$ is a CQG. To conclude the proof of $(1)$ we only have to check the last condition of \cite[Definition 1.1]{FP16}. To do so, we use \cite[Remark 1]{FP16}. Let, for $v\in\mathrm{Rep}(G)$, $s_v\in\mathrm{Mor}_G(1,v\otimes\overline{v})$ and $s_{\overline{v}}\in\mathrm{Mor}_G(1,\overline{v}\otimes v)$ be a pair solving the conjugate equation for $(v,\overline{v})$. Since $\eta\in\mathrm{Mor}_H(1,u)$, $a(1)=u$, assertion $(6)$ gives:
$$S_v:=\Sigma_{23}(s_v\otimes m^\star)\eta\in\mathrm{Mor}(1,a(v)\otimes a(\overline{v}))\quad\text{and}\quad S_{\overline{v}}:=\Sigma_{23}(s_{\overline{v}}\otimes m^\star)\eta\in\mathrm{Mor}(1,a({\overline{v}})\otimes a(v)).$$
Suppose that the pair $(s_v,s_{\overline{v}})$ is standard. To show that $(C(\mathbb{G}),\Delta)$ is a CQG it remains to prove that $S_{\overline{v}}$ is non-degenerated in the sense of \cite[Remark 1]{FP16}. Writing, as in Section \ref{SectionCQG}, $s_{\overline{v}}=\sum_iQ_{v,i}^{-\frac{1}{2}}e_i^{\overline{v}}\otimes e_i^{v}$ we find, as in the proof of \cite[Proposition 2.7]{FP16}, and using the notations introduced at the end of Section \ref{SectionQAut},
$$S_{\overline{v}}=\sum_{\kappa,i,j,k}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{\kappa,j}}{Q_{v,i}\lambda_{\kappa,k}}}e^{\overline{v}}_i\otimes b^\kappa_{jk}\otimes e^v_i\otimes b^\kappa_{kj}.$$
From this formula, it is clear that $S_{\overline{v}}$ is non-degenerated so $(C(\mathbb{G}),\Delta)$ is a CQG. The same computation gives $S_v=\sum_{\kappa,i,j,k}\sqrt{\frac{Q_{v,i}\lambda_{\kappa,j}}{\lambda_{\kappa,k}}}e^v_i\otimes b^\kappa_{jk}\otimes e^{\overline{v}}_i\otimes b^\kappa_{kj}$. From these formulas, one checks easily that the pair $(S_v,S_{\overline{v}})$ solves the conjugate equation for $(a(v),a(\overline{v}))$ so $\overline{a(v)}\simeq a(\overline{v})$ for all $v\in\mathrm{Rep}(G)$. 

\vspace{0.2cm}

\noindent Note that statement  $(4)$ is an easy consequence of the fact that $\rho(f)=1_B\otimes f$ for all $f\in C(F)$. Finally, the existence and uniqueness of the character $\varepsilon_\mathbb{G}$ satisfying the properties given in $(2)$ is a direct consequence of the universal property of $C(\mathbb{G})$. The fact that it is the counit of $\mathbb{G}$ follows from the definition of $\Delta$ and $\varepsilon_\mathbb{G}$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
The CQG $\mathbb{G}$ constructed above is called \textit{the generalized free wreath product} of $G$ and $(H,\beta)$, amalgamated on $F$, and denoted by $G\wr_{*,\beta,F}H$. When $F$ is the trivial group, we call it the generalized free wreath product of $G$ and $(H,\beta)$, denoted $G\wr_{*,\beta}H$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\label{RmkFwp}The following statements are easy to check.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $F$ is equal to $G$ i.e. the inclusion $C(F)\subset C(G)$ is surjective, then $G\wr_{*,\beta,F}H \simeq G \times H$.
    \item The canonical surjection $\pi_H:=({\rm id}\otimes\varepsilon_G)\pi\,:\,C(\mathbb{G})\rightarrow C(H)$, where $\pi$ is constructed in Remark \ref{RmkIota} intertwines the comultiplications so $H$ is a compact quantum subgroup of $\mathbb{G}$. Hence $H$ is both a quantum subgroup and a dual quantum subgroup of $\mathbb{G}$.
    \item There exists a unique unital $*$-homomorphism $\pi_G\,:\, C(\mathbb{G})\rightarrow C(G)^{\ast K}$ such that, for all $a\in C(G)$, $({\rm id}\otimes\pi_G)\rho(a)= \sum_{\kappa=1}^K 1_\kappa \otimes a$ and $\pi_G\vert_{C(H)}=\varepsilon_H(\cdot)1$. Moreover, $\pi_G$ is easily seen to be surjective and intertwines the comultiplications. Hence $G^{\ast K}$ is a compact quantum subgroup of $\mathbb{G}$.
    \item If $\beta$ is the trivial action $B\rightarrow B\otimes C(H)$ i.e. $\beta(b)=b\otimes 1$ then: $$G\wr_{*,\beta,F}H=(G^{\ast_F K}) \underset{F}{*} (H\times F).$$
    \item  Suppose that $\beta_k\,:\, B_k\rightarrow B_k\otimes C(H_k)$, $k=1,2$, two $\psi_k$-preserving actions, are \textit{isomorphic} in the sense that there exist two isomorphisms $\pi\,:\, B_1\rightarrow B_2$ and $\varphi\,:\, H_1\rightarrow H_2$ such that $\psi_2\circ\pi=\psi_1$ and $\beta_2\circ\pi=(\pi\otimes\varphi)\beta_1$. Then, $$G\wr_{*,\beta_1,F}H_1\simeq G\wr_{*,\beta_2,F}H_2.$$
\item If we have a pair of dual quantum subgroups of $G$ , $\mathbb{C} 1_G \subset C(F_1) \subset C(F_2) \subset C(G)$, then we get surjective unital $*$-homomorphisms: $$ C(G\wr_{\ast,\beta}H) \rightarrow C(G\wr_{\ast,\beta,F_1} H) \rightarrow C(G\wr_{\ast,\beta,F_2} H) \rightarrow C(G\wr_{\ast,\beta,G} H) \simeq C(G)\otimes_{{\rm max}} C(H),$$ all of these morphisms intertwining the comultiplications. The last isomorphism is the one from $(1)$, in the case of the amalgamation on $G$ itself.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{Propfaithful}
Denoting by $H_0$ the dual quantum subgroup of $H$ generated by the coefficients of $u$, there is an isomorphism $G\wr_{*,\beta,F}H \simeq (G\wr_{*,\beta,F}H_0) \underset{H_0 \times F}{\ast}(H\times F)$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let us denote by $\rho_0$ the map defining $\mathbb{G}_0:=G\wr_{*,\beta,F}H_0$, $\rho$ the one for $\mathbb{G}:=G\wr_{*,\beta,F}H$ and view $C(H_0\times F)\subset C(\mathbb{G}_0)$ and $C(H\times F)\subset C(\mathbb{G})$. Define $\Sigma:=\mathbb{G}_0\underset{H_0 \times F}{\ast}(H\times F)$ and view $C(\mathbb{G}_0),C(H\times F)\subset C(\Sigma)$. By the universal property of $C(\mathbb{G})$, there is a unique unital $*$-homomorphism $\pi\,:\, C(\mathbb{G})\rightarrow C(\Sigma)$ such that:
$$({\rm id}\otimes\pi)\rho=\rho_0\,:\, C(G)\rightarrow B\otimes C(\mathbb{G}_0)\subset B\otimes C(\Sigma)\text{ and }\pi\vert_{C(H\times F)}\text{ is the inclusion}.$$
It is easy to check that $\pi$ intertwines the comultiplication. Moreover, the universal property of $C(\mathbb{G}_0)$ gives a unique unital $*$-homomorphism $\pi_0\,:\,C(\mathbb{G}_0)\rightarrow C(\mathbb{G})$ such that $({\rm id}\otimes\pi_0)\rho_0=\rho$ and $\pi_0\vert_{C(H_0\times F)}$ is the inclusion $C(H_0\times F)\subset C(H\times F)\subset C(\mathbb{G})$. Now, by the universal property of the amalgamated free product $C(\Sigma)=C(\mathbb{G}_0)\underset{C(H_0\times F)}{*}C(H\times F)$, there is a unique unital $*$-homomorphism $\pi^{-1}\,:\, C(\Sigma)\rightarrow C(\mathbb{G})$ such that $\pi^{-1}\vert_{C(\mathbb{G}_0)}=\pi_0$ and $\pi\vert_{C(H\times F)}$ is the inclusion $C(H\times F)\subset C(\mathbb{G})$. It is clear that $\pi^{-1}$ is the inverse of $\pi$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{PropSemiDirect}
If $\Lambda\curvearrowright X$ is free then there is a canonical isomorphism $$G\wr_{*,\beta,F}\Lambda\simeq G^{*_F X\times K}\rtimes\Lambda,$$
where $X\times K:=X\times\{1,\dots,K\}$ and the action $\Lambda\curvearrowright X\times K$ is given by $\gamma\cdot(x,\kappa):=(\gamma\cdot x,\kappa)$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let $\mathbb{G}:=G\wr_{*,\beta,F}\Lambda$. Recall that $C(G^{*_F X}\rtimes\Lambda)=C(G^{*_F X})\otimes C(\Lambda)$ and define $\rho\,:\,C(G)\rightarrow B^X\otimes C(G^{*_F X\times K})\subset B^X\otimes C(G^{*_F X\times K}\rtimes\Lambda)$ by $\rho(a):=\sum_{x\in X,1\leq\kappa\leq K}e_{x,\kappa}\otimes\nu_{x,\kappa}(a)$ and both $\iota_F\,:\,C(F)\rightarrow C(G^{*_F X\times K})\subset C(G^{*_F X\times K}\rtimes\Lambda)$ and $\iota_\Lambda\,:\, C(\Lambda)\rightarrow C(G^{*_F X}\rtimes\Lambda)$ are the inclusions. It is clear that they satisfy the relations of $C(\mathbb{G})$. Moreover, with these maps, $C(G^{*_F X\times F}\rtimes\Lambda)$ satisfies the universal property of $C(\mathbb{G})$. Indeed, if $\pi\,:\, C(G)\rightarrow B^X\otimes C$, $\iota'_F\,:\, C(F)\rightarrow C$ and $\iota'_\Lambda\,:\, C(\Lambda)\rightarrow C$ are unital $*$-homomorphisms such that
$$\pi(f)=1_{B^X}\otimes\iota'_F(f), \,\,[\pi(a),({\rm id}\otimes\iota'_\Lambda)(\beta(b))]=0, \,\,[\iota'_\Lambda(c),\iota'_F(f)]=0$$
for all $a\in C(G)$, $b\in B^X$, $c\in C(\Lambda)$ and $f\in C(F)$. Writing $\pi(a)=\sum_{x,\kappa,i,j} e^{x,\kappa}_{ij}\otimes\pi_{ij}^{x,\kappa}(a)$ and applying $(\chi_x\otimes {\rm id})$ to the relation $[\pi(a),({\rm id}\otimes\iota'_\Lambda)(\beta(b))]=0$ we find, for all $x\in X$, $a\in C(G)$ and $b\in B^X$,
$$\sum_{\kappa,i,j,\gamma}e^\kappa_{ij}\chi_{\gamma^{-1}\cdot x}(b)\otimes\pi^{x,\kappa}_{ij}(a)\iota_\Lambda'(\delta_\gamma)=\sum_{\kappa,i,j,\gamma}\chi_{\gamma^{-1}\cdot x}(b)e^\kappa_{ij}\otimes\iota_\Lambda'(\delta_\gamma)\pi^{x,\kappa}_{ij}(a).$$
Fix any $\kappa, r,s$ and $y\in X$ and apply this equation to $b:=e^{\kappa,y}_{rs}\in B^X$ to get:
$$\sum_{i}e^\kappa_{is}\otimes\pi^{x,\kappa}_{ir}(a)\iota'_\Lambda(u_{xy})=\sum_{j}e^\kappa_{rj}\otimes\iota'_\Lambda(u_{xy})\pi_{sj}^{x,\kappa}(a),$$
where $u_{xy}:=1_{\{\gamma\in\Lambda\,:\,\gamma\cdot y=x\}}$. This implies that, for all $\kappa,i,r$, all $a\in C(G)$ and all $x,y\in X$,
\begin{equation}\label{EqCummutation}\pi^{x,\kappa}_{ir}(a)\iota'_\Lambda(u_{xy})=\delta_{ir}\iota'_\Lambda(u_{xy})\pi^{x,\kappa}_{ss}(a).\end{equation}
Since $1=\sum_yu_{xy}\in C(\Lambda)$, for all $x\in X$, we deduce in particular that $\pi^{x,\kappa}_{ir}(a)=\delta_{ir}\pi^{x,\kappa}_{ss}(a)$ for all $x,\kappa,i,r,s,a$. For $a\in C(G)$ let $\pi_{x,\kappa}(a)\in C$ be the element satisfying $\pi_{x,\kappa}(a)=\pi^{x,\kappa}_{rr}(a)$ for all $1\leq r\leq N_\kappa$ and note that $\pi$ is of the form:
$$\pi(a)=\sum_{x,\kappa,r}e^{x,\kappa}_{rr}\otimes\pi_{x,\kappa}(a)=\sum_{x,\kappa}e_{x,\kappa}\otimes\pi_{x,\kappa}(a),$$
Since the projections $e_{x,\kappa}$ are pairwise orthogonal and $\pi$ is a unital $*$-homomorphism, each $\pi_{x,\kappa}\,:\,C(G)\rightarrow C$ is a unital $*$-homomorphism and, since $\pi(f)=1_{B^X}\otimes\iota'_F(f)$, we have $\pi_{x,\kappa}(f)=\iota'_F(f)$ for all $f\in F$. Moreover, Equation $(\ref{EqCummutation})$ also implies that, for all  $a\in C(G)$ and all $x,y\in X$ and all $1\leq\kappa\leq K$, $\pi_{x,\kappa}(a)\iota'_\Lambda(u_{xy})=\iota'_\Lambda(u_{xy})\pi_{x,\kappa}(a)$. Hence, for all $a\in C(G)$ and $(x,\kappa)\in X\times K$, $\pi_{x,\kappa}(a)$ commutes with $\iota'_\Lambda(c)$ for all $c\in\mathcal{A}_x$, where $\mathcal{A}_x\subset C(\Lambda)$ is the unital $*$-algebra generated by $\{u_{xy}\,:\, y\in X\}$. Since the action $\Lambda\curvearrowright X$ is free, $\mathcal{A}_x$ separates the points of $\Lambda$ and so $\mathcal{A}_x=C(\Lambda)$, for all $x\in X$. This implies that for all $a\in A$, $(x,\kappa)\in X\times K$ and $c\in C(\Lambda)$ $[\pi_{x,\kappa}(a),\iota'_\Lambda(c)]=0$. Hence, there exists a unique unital $*$-homomorphism $\widetilde{\pi}\,:\, C(G^{*_FX\times K})\otimes C(\Lambda)\rightarrow C$ such that $\widetilde{\pi}\circ\nu_{x,\kappa}=\pi_{x,\kappa}$ and $\widetilde{\pi}\circ\iota'_\Lambda=\iota_\Lambda$. This shows the universal property hence we may and will assume that $C(\mathbb{G})=C(G^{*_F X\times K})\otimes C(\Lambda)$ with maps $\rho$, $\iota_\Lambda$ and $\iota_F$ given above. Let us denote by $\Delta_1$ the comultiplication on $C(\mathbb{G})$ given by the free wreath product construction and by $\Delta_2$ the one given by the semi-direct product construction. It suffices to show that $\Delta_1=\Delta_2$. Since by construction, they both coincide with $\Delta_\Lambda$ on $C(\Lambda)$, it suffices to show that $\Delta_1\circ\nu_{x,\kappa}=\Delta_2\circ\nu_{x,\kappa}$ for all $(x,\kappa)\in X\times K$. Note that, for all $a\in{\rm Pol}(G)$,  $\Delta_2(\nu_{x,\kappa}(a))=\sum_{\gamma\in\Lambda}\nu_{x,\kappa}(a_{(1)})\iota_\Lambda(\delta_\gamma)\otimes\nu_{\gamma^{-1}\cdot x,\kappa}(a_{(2)})$ and,
\begin{eqnarray*}
({\rm id}\otimes\Delta_1)(\rho(a))&=&\sum_{x,\kappa} e_{x,\kappa}\otimes\Delta_1(\nu_{x,\kappa}(a))=(\beta_G\otimes{\rm id})({\rm id}\otimes\rho)\Delta_G(a)
\\
&=&\sum\beta_G(a_{(1)}\otimes e_{y,\zeta})\otimes\nu_{y,\zeta}(a_{(2)})=\sum\rho(a_{(1)})\beta(e_{y,\zeta})\otimes\nu_{y,\zeta}(a_{(2)})\\
&=&\sum e_{x,\kappa}e_{\gamma\cdot y,\zeta}\otimes\nu_{x,\kappa}(a_{(1)})\iota_\Lambda(\delta_\gamma)\otimes\nu_{y,\zeta}(a_{(2)})\\
&=&\sum e_{x,\kappa}\otimes\nu_{x,\kappa}(a_{(1)})\iota_\Lambda(\delta_\gamma)\otimes\nu_{\gamma^{-1}\cdot x,\kappa}(a_{(2)})
\end{eqnarray*}
It follows that $\Delta_1\circ\nu_{x,\kappa}=\Delta_2\circ\nu_{x,\kappa}$ for all $(x,\kappa)\in X\times K$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
Gromada's wreath product \cite{Gr23} is a particular case of generalized free wreath products: this follows from Proposition \ref{PropSemiDirect} (with $B=\mathbb{C}$) and \cite[Proposition 2.27]{FT24}.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{PropBichon}
Let $G$ be a compact quantum group with a dual quantum subgroup $F$. For the universal action $\beta\,:\, S_N^+\curvearrowright\mathbb{C}^N$ there is a canonical isomorphism $G\wr_{*,\beta,F} S_N^+\simeq G\wr_{*,F}S_N^+$, where $G\wr_{*,F}S_N^+$ denotes the free wreath product from \cite{Fr22}.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
There is a unique $*$-isomorphism $\pi\,:\, C(G\wr_*{\rm Aut}^+(B,\psi))\rightarrow C(G\wr_{*,\beta}{\rm Aut}^+(B,\psi))$ such that $({\rm id}\otimes\pi)(r(x))=a(u^x)\in\mathcal{L}(H_x)\otimes\mathcal{L}(B)\otimes C(\mathbb{G})$ for all $x\in{\rm Irr}(G)$. Moreover, $\pi$ intertwines the comultiplications.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The uniqueness is clear and the existence of $\pi$ is a direct consequence of the universal property of $C(G\wr_*{\rm Aut}^+(B,\psi))$ and assertion $(6)$ of Theorem \ref{ThmDefFreeWr}. It is clear that $\pi$ intertwines the comultiplications since $a(u^x)$ is a unitary representation. Let us construct the inverse of $\pi$. By the universal property of $C(G)$ and \cite[Proposition 8.1]{FP16} there exists a unique unital $*$-homomorphism $\varphi_0\,:\,C(G)\rightarrow B\otimes C(G\wr_*{\rm Aut}^+(B,\psi))$ such that $$({\rm id}\otimes\varphi_0)(v)=r'(v):=r(v)({\rm id}\otimes 1_B\otimes 1)\text{ for all }v\in\mathrm{Rep}(G),$$
where $r(v)$, for non irreducible $v\in\mathrm{Rep}(G)$, is defined just before \cite[Proposition 8.1]{FP16} (denoted there $a(v)$). By the universal property of $C({\rm Aut}^+(B,\psi))$ there is a unique unital $*$-homomorphism  $\iota_B\,:\,C({\rm Aut}^+(B,\psi))\rightarrow C(G\wr_*{\rm Aut}^+(B,\psi))$ such that $({\rm id}\otimes\iota_B)(u)=r(1)$. From \cite[Proposition 8.1]{FP16} we know that $({\rm id}_{H_v}\otimes m)\in\mathrm{Mor}_{G\wr_*{\rm Aut}^+(B,\psi)}(r(v)\otimes r(1),r(v))$ and $({\rm id}_{H_v}\otimes m)\Sigma_{12}\in\mathrm{Mor}_{G\wr_*{\rm Aut}^+(B,\psi)}(r(1)\otimes r(v),r(v))$. Hence,

\begin{eqnarray*}
({\rm id}_{H_v}\otimes m\otimes 1)r(v)_{124}r(1)_{34}&=&r(v)({\rm id}_{H_v}\otimes m\otimes 1)\\
&=&(({\rm id}_{H_v}\otimes m)\Sigma_{12}\otimes 1)r(1)_{14}r(v)_{234}(\Sigma_{12}\otimes 1)\\
&=&({\rm id}_{H_v}\otimes m\otimes 1)r(1)_{24} r(v)_{134}
\end{eqnarray*}

\noindent Take an orthonormal basis $(e_r)_r$ of $H_v$ with matrix units $(e_{rs})_{rs}$ in $\mathcal{L}(H_v)$, write $v=\sum_{r,s}e_{rs}\otimes v_{rs}$ and:
$$r(v)=\sum_{r,s,i,j,\kappa,k,l,\zeta}e_{rs}\otimes b_{ij}^\kappa\circ (b_{kl}^\zeta)^\star\otimes r(v)^{ij,\kappa}_{kl,\zeta,rs}\quad r(1)=\sum_{i,j,\kappa,k,l,\zeta} b_{ij}^\kappa\circ (b_{kl}^\zeta)^\star\otimes r(1)^{ij,\kappa}_{kl,\zeta,rs}.$$
Note that $\sum_{\gamma,r}\lambda_{\gamma,r}^{\frac{1}{2}}r(1)^{ij,\kappa}_{rr,\gamma}=\delta_{ij}\lambda_{\kappa,i}^{\frac{1}{2}}$, since $\iota_B$ is a unital $*$-homomorphism. From the relation $b^\kappa_{ip}b^{\zeta}_{qj}=\delta_{\kappa\zeta}\delta_{pq}\lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}}_{\kappa,p}b^\kappa_{ij}$ we find $m\circ (b^\kappa_{ip}\circ (b^\zeta_{kl})^\star\otimes b^{\kappa'}_{qj}\circ (b^{\zeta'}_{k'l'})^\star)=\delta_{\kappa,\kappa'}\delta_{p,q}\lambda_{\kappa,p}^{-1/2}b^\kappa_{ij}\circ  ((b^\zeta_{kl})^\star\otimes (b^{\zeta'}_{k'l'})^\star)$.

\vspace{0.2cm}

\noindent It follows that $({\rm id}_{H_v}\otimes m\otimes 1)r(v)_{124}r(1)_{34}$ is equal to:
$$\sum e_{rs}\otimes b^\kappa_{ij}\circ((b^\zeta_{kl})^\star\otimes(b^{\zeta'}_{k'l'})^\star)\otimes\left(\sum_p\lambda_{\kappa,p}^{-1/2}r(v)^{ip,\kappa}_{kl,\zeta,rs}r(1)^{pj,\kappa}_{k'l',\zeta'}\right),$$
and $({\rm id}_{H_v}\otimes m\otimes 1)r(1)_{24}r(v)_{134}$ is equal to:
$$\sum e_{rs}\otimes b^\kappa_{ij}\circ((b^\zeta_{kl})^\star\otimes(b^{\zeta'}_{k'l'})^\star)\otimes\left(\sum_p\lambda_{\kappa,p}^{-1/2}r(1)^{ip,\kappa}_{kl,\zeta}r(v)^{pj,\kappa}_{k'l',\zeta',rs}\right).$$

\noindent Then, for all $r,s,\kappa,i,j,\zeta,k,l,\zeta',k',l'$ one has

\begin{equation}\label{Eqfwp1}
\sum_p\lambda_{\kappa,p}^{-1/2}r(v)^{ip,\kappa}_{kl,\zeta,rs}r(1)^{pj,\kappa}_{k'l',\zeta'}=\sum_p\lambda_{\kappa,p}^{-1/2}r(1)^{ip,\kappa}_{kl,\zeta}r(v)^{pj,\kappa}_{k'l',\zeta',rs}.
\end{equation}

\noindent Note that $(b_{kl}^\zeta)^\star(1_B)=\psi((b_{kl}^\zeta)^*)=\delta_{kl}\lambda_{\zeta,k}^{1/2}$ hence,
$$r'(v)=\sum e_{rs}\otimes b_{ij}^\kappa\circ (b_{kl}^\zeta)^\star(1_B)\otimes r(v)^{ij,\kappa}_{kl,\zeta,rs}=\sum e_{rs}\otimes b_{ij}^\kappa\otimes  \lambda_{\zeta,k}^{1/2} r(v)^{ij,\kappa}_{kk,\zeta,rs}.$$
\noindent It follows that $\varphi_0(v_{rs})=\sum b_{ij}^\kappa\otimes  \lambda_{\zeta,q}^{1/2} r(v)^{ij,\kappa}_{qq,\zeta,rs}$. Writing $\beta(b^\alpha_{kl})=\sum_{\kappa,i,j}b^\kappa_{ij}\otimes u^{ij,\kappa}_{kl,\alpha}$ and using Equation $(\ref{Eqfwp1})$ we deduce that, with $X:=({\rm id}\otimes\iota_B)(\beta(b^\alpha_{kl}))\varphi_0(v_{rs})$,

\begin{eqnarray*}
X&=&\sum b^\kappa_{ij}\otimes\sum_{p,\zeta,q}\left(\frac{\lambda_{\zeta,q}}{\lambda_{\kappa,p}}\right)^{1/2}r(1)^{ip,\kappa}_{kl,\alpha}r(v)^{pj,\kappa}_{qq,\zeta,rs}
=\sum b^\kappa_{ij}\otimes\sum_{p,\zeta,q}\left(\frac{\lambda_{\zeta,q}}{\lambda_{\kappa,p}}\right)^{1/2}r(v)^{ip,\kappa}_{kl,\alpha,rs}r(1)^{pj,\kappa}_{qq,\zeta}\\
&=&\sum b^\kappa_{ij}\otimes\sum_{p}\lambda_{\kappa,p}^{-1/2}r(v)^{ip,\kappa}_{kl,\alpha,rs}\left(\sum_{\zeta,q}\lambda_{\zeta,q}^{1/2}r(1)^{pj,\kappa}_{qq,\zeta}\right)=\sum b^\kappa_{ij}\otimes r(v)^{ij,\kappa}_{kl,\alpha,rs}.
\end{eqnarray*}

\noindent The same computation with $Y:=\varphi_0(v_{rs})({\rm id}\otimes\iota_B)(\beta(b^\alpha_{kl}))$ gives:

\begin{eqnarray*}
Y&=&\sum b^\kappa_{ij}\otimes\sum_{p,\zeta,q}\left(\frac{\lambda_{\zeta,q}}{\lambda_{\kappa,p}}\right)^{1/2}r(v)^{ip,\kappa}_{qq,\zeta,rs}r(1)^{pj,\kappa}_{kl,\alpha}
=\sum b^\kappa_{ij}\otimes\sum_{p,\zeta,q}\left(\frac{\lambda_{\zeta,q}}{\lambda_{\kappa,p}}\right)^{1/2}r(1)^{ip,\kappa}_{qq,\zeta}r(v)^{pj,\kappa}_{kl,\alpha,rs}\\
&=&\sum b^\kappa_{ij}\otimes\sum_{p}\lambda_{\kappa,p}^{-1/2}\left(\sum_{\zeta,q}\lambda_{\zeta,q}^{1/2}r(1)^{ip,\kappa}_{qq,\zeta}\right)r(v)^{pj,\kappa}_{kl,\alpha,rs}=\sum b^\kappa_{ij}\otimes r(v)^{ij,\kappa}_{kl,\alpha,rs}.
\end{eqnarray*}

\noindent Hence, $({\rm id}\otimes\iota_B)(\beta(b^\alpha_{kl}))\varphi_0(v_{rs})=\varphi_0(v_{rs})({\rm id}\otimes\iota_B)(\beta(b^\alpha_{kl}))$ and since this holds for any $v\in\mathrm{Rep}(G)$ and any $\zeta,k,l$, we deduce that $[\varphi_0(a),({\rm id}\otimes\iota_B)(\beta(b))]=0$ for all $a\in C(G)$ and all $b\in B$.
